core.q: A container's liveness probe fails and the kubelet declares it unhealthy. What actually happens to the Pod?
o: The kubelet kills and restarts only that container in place; the Pod keeps its name, IP, and node assignment
The endpoints controller removes the Pod's IP from the Service's EndpointSlices, but the container keeps running
The Pod is deleted and rescheduled to a different node by the scheduler
The container is throttled by the CFS quota until it recovers
core.x: A failed liveness probe only restarts the individual container in place; the Pod object, IP, and node survive. Removing endpoints on failure is what readiness does instead.
core.t: Interviewers hope you'll say 'the pod restarts' — it doesn't.

core.q:
You run `kubectl describe pod web-0` and see:
Last State: Terminated
  Reason: OOMKilled
  Exit Code: 137
What does this tell you?
o: The container exceeded its CPU limit and was throttled
The container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel OOM killer killed it
The container received SIGTERM during a graceful pod deletion
The liveness probe failed and the kubelet restarted the container
core.x: Exit code 137 with reason OOMKilled means the process allocated past its memory limit and the kernel OOM killer terminated it; CPU limits only throttle, they never kill.

core.q: Why does a Pod need a hidden 'pause' (infrastructure) container?
o: To enforce CPU/memory limits via cgroups
To run health checks independent of the app container
To hold open the shared network/IPC namespaces so app containers can join them and the Pod IP survives an app container restart
To provide DNS resolution for the Pod
core.x: The pause container owns the Pod's network and IPC namespaces; app containers join those namespaces, which is mechanically why the Pod IP survives an app container crashing and restarting.

core.q: Your team sets failureThreshold: 30 and periodSeconds: 10 on a startupProbe for a slow-booting JVM app. What is the effective startup budget, and what happens to the other probes during that window?
o: 60 seconds; liveness runs normally throughout
300 seconds; readiness runs but liveness is suspended
30 seconds; both probes run in parallel with the startup probe
300 seconds; both liveness and readiness are suppressed until the startup probe succeeds once
core.x: The startup budget is failureThreshold x periodSeconds = 30 x 10s = 300s, and a startup probe suppresses both liveness and readiness until it succeeds once.

core.q: A Pod has an init container and a native sidecar (log-shipper with restartPolicy: Always) ahead of the main app container. In what order do they start, and does the kubelet wait for the sidecar to exit before starting the app?
o: Init container runs to completion first, the sidecar starts next and is not waited on to exit — the app starts once the sidecar is launched
All three start simultaneously
Sidecar and app start together, and the init container runs last
The kubelet waits for the sidecar to exit before starting the app container
core.x: A native sidecar is an init container with restartPolicy: Always — the kubelet starts it in init order but doesn't wait for it to exit, and keeps it running for the Pod's life.

core.q: A node is under memory pressure and the kubelet must evict pods. Pod A has requests equal to limits for CPU and memory (Guaranteed QoS). Pod B has no requests or limits set at all (BestEffort). Which is evicted first?
o: Pod A, because Guaranteed pods are evicted first to protect capacity
Pod B, because BestEffort pods are evicted before Burstable and Guaranteed pods
Both are evicted simultaneously since QoS doesn't affect eviction order
Neither — eviction order depends only on pod age
core.x: QoS class governs eviction order under node pressure: BestEffort pods go first, then Burstable pods exceeding requests, and Guaranteed pods are evicted last.

core.q: kubectl get pod shows Phase: Running, but kubectl describe shows a container state of Waiting with reason CrashLoopBackOff. What should you conclude?
o: The Pod phase is wrong; Kubernetes has a bug reporting Running incorrectly
The container passed its liveness probe and is healthy
Pod phase is a coarse summary and can show Running even while a container is Waiting/crash-looping; check per-container state and kubectl logs --previous
This is only possible if the readiness probe is misconfigured
core.x: Pod phase is a coarse rollup while container states carry the actionable detail — 'the pod says Running' proves very little on its own.

core.q:
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/web
Waiting for deployment "web" rollout to finish: 3 out of 10 new replicas have been updated...

$ kubectl get deploy web -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Progressing")].reason}'
ProgressDeadlineExceeded

What is the correct diagnosis, and will Kubernetes fix it automatically?
o: The rollout is paused; resume it with kubectl rollout resume
maxUnavailable is set too low; increase it and the rollout will finish
The old ReplicaSet was garbage collected; nothing can be done
The rollout is stuck (e.g. a bad image or failing readiness) and exceeded progressDeadlineSeconds; Kubernetes will NOT auto-rollback — fix with kubectl rollout undo or a corrected image
core.x: A stuck rollout only flips the Progressing condition to False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded after the default 600s deadline; Kubernetes never rolls back on its own.

core.q: You run `kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=20`. Does this trigger a new ReplicaSet and rolling update?
o: No — only changes to .spec.template trigger a new ReplicaSet; replica count changes do not
Yes — any change to the Deployment object creates a new revision
Yes, but only if maxSurge is greater than 0
No, because scale operations bypass the Deployment controller entirely
core.x: Only a change to .spec.template changes the pod-template-hash and creates a new ReplicaSet/revision; scaling replicas does not.

core.q: You set revisionHistoryLimit: 0 on a Deployment. Weeks later a bad release ships and you try kubectl rollout undo. What happens?
o: It works normally; revisionHistoryLimit only affects kubectl rollout history output
Rollback is impossible — the old ReplicaSets holding prior templates were garbage collected
Kubernetes automatically restores revision 1 regardless of the limit
The Deployment reverts to its default template
core.x: Rollback works by scaling an old ReplicaSet back up; revisionHistoryLimit: 0 lets those old ReplicaSets be garbage-collected, silently destroying rollback ability.

core.q: Why does a StatefulSet require a headless Service (clusterIP: None)?
o: To load-balance traffic evenly across replicas
To let the scheduler assign stable node names
To provide the stable per-pod DNS record <pod>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local that clustered apps use to find peers
To automatically encrypt traffic between replicas
core.x: The headless Service is what gives each ordinal a stable DNS record, which is exactly what clustered systems like Kafka or PostgreSQL need to find their peers.

core.q: You scale a StatefulSet from 5 replicas down to 0 and back up to 5. What happens to the PVCs created via volumeClaimTemplates?
o: They are deleted on scale-down and recreated empty on scale-up
They are merged into a single shared PVC
They are deleted only if persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy is unset
They are NOT deleted by default; each ordinal reattaches its original PVC (e.g. web-1 remounts www-web-1) with its old data
core.x: PVC binding is sticky and PVCs are not deleted by default even when the StatefulSet is scaled down or deleted — a deliberate data-safety choice.

core.q: A 3-replica StatefulSet with the default podManagementPolicy is mid-rollout and web-0 crashloops on the new image. What happens to web-1 and web-2?
o: The rollout wedges — with OrderedReady, later ordinals are never touched until web-0 becomes Ready
They update anyway since StatefulSets always update in parallel
They roll back automatically
They are deleted to make room for a healthy web-0
core.x: With the default OrderedReady policy, pods are created and updated strictly in order — a crashlooping web-0 wedges the entire rollout.

core.q: A DaemonSet runs a log-shipping agent. Why do its pods keep running on a node that is being drained of ordinary workloads?
o: DaemonSet pods run with root privileges that exempt them from draining
The controller automatically adds tolerations for node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and unreachable, keeping DaemonSet pods on nodes ordinary workloads are evicted from
DaemonSets are excluded from node affinity rules entirely
kubectl drain never affects any pod by design
core.x: The DaemonSet controller adds tolerations for node lifecycle taints automatically, which is why log agents and CNI plugins keep running on nodes ordinary workloads are being evicted from.

core.q:
kubectl describe pod shows:
Events:
  Warning  FailedScheduling  0/5 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu, 2 node(s) had untolerated taint {dedicated: gpu}
What two independent fixes map to these two failure reasons?
o: Add more replicas; change the Service type
Increase the liveness probe timeout; change restartPolicy
Lower CPU requests or add nodes for the Insufficient cpu nodes; add a toleration or remove the taint for the tainted nodes
Enable preemptionPolicy: Never; delete the PriorityClass
core.x: Each named filter in a FailedScheduling event maps one-to-one to a fix: resource shortfalls need lower requests or more nodes, taint mismatches need a toleration or taint removal.

core.q: Which statement correctly describes how the scheduler uses requests versus limits?
o: The scheduler sums limits across pods to decide node fit
The scheduler uses live resource usage (kubectl top) to decide node fit
The scheduler ignores both and relies on the kubelet to reject overloaded pods
The scheduler only looks at requests; limits are enforced later by the kernel, not consulted for placement
core.x: The scheduler fits pods onto nodes using only requests; limits are a kernel-enforced ceiling checked later, never part of the placement decision.
core.t: Classically confused with limits — the scheduler never looks at limits or live usage.

core.q: A container exceeds its CPU limit under load. What happens to it, versus a container that exceeds its memory limit?
o: The CPU-limited container is throttled by the CFS quota (slows down, never killed); the memory-limited container is OOMKilled by the kernel (exit 137)
Both are OOMKilled immediately
Both are throttled without being killed
The CPU-limited container is OOMKilled; the memory-limited container is throttled
core.x: CPU is a compressible resource enforced via CFS quota (throttling); memory is incompressible, so exceeding its limit triggers the kernel OOM killer.
core.h: CPU is compressible, memory is not.
core.t: The tempting wrong answer is 'it gets killed' for CPU — that's only true for memory.

core.q: A required podAntiAffinity on topology.kubernetes.io/hostname is set for a 4-replica Deployment running on a 3-node cluster. What happens to the 4th replica?
o: It preempts a lower-priority pod on one of the 3 nodes
It stays Pending forever — the constraint is unsatisfiable with only 3 nodes
It is scheduled onto a node already hosting a replica, ignoring the constraint
The scheduler automatically relaxes hard anti-affinity after a timeout
core.x: Required (hard) anti-affinity that can't be satisfied leaves the pod Pending forever; nothing is broken, the constraint is simply unsatisfiable given the node count.

core.q: You taint a node dedicated=batch:NoSchedule and add a matching toleration to your batch pods, but you set no nodeAffinity. What's wrong with expecting the pods to land only on that node?
o: NoSchedule taints require an explicit nodeSelector to have any effect at all
Tolerations are ignored unless combined with a PriorityClass
A toleration only unlocks the door — it doesn't pull the pod there; without nodeAffinity the pods may still land on general nodes
NoSchedule taints don't apply to Deployments, only to bare Pods
core.x: Dedicated node pools need both the taint (to repel other workloads) and matching nodeAffinity (to attract your workloads); a toleration alone never steers a pod there.

core.q: What is the key difference in effect between a NoSchedule taint and a NoExecute taint?
o: NoSchedule is a hard filter and NoExecute is only a scoring preference
NoExecute only applies to DaemonSets
NoSchedule evicts running pods; NoExecute only blocks new placements
NoSchedule blocks new placements but leaves running pods alone; NoExecute additionally evicts already-running pods lacking a matching toleration
core.x: Taint effects escalate: NoSchedule only blocks new placement, while NoExecute also evicts pods already running there unless they tolerate it (optionally after tolerationSeconds).
core.t: Commonly swapped in interviews — remember NoExecute is the one that evicts.

core.q: A node stops heartbeating and goes NotReady. Roughly how long until its pods are evicted and replacements scheduled elsewhere, and what mechanism causes it?
o: About 300 seconds — the node controller adds node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute, and pods have a default 300s toleration for it before eviction
Immediately — NotReady nodes have their pods evicted within seconds
Never automatically — an operator must manually cordon and drain the node
40 seconds, matching the node heartbeat timeout exactly
core.x: The node controller marks the node NotReady around 40s after it stops heartbeating and taints it unreachable:NoExecute; pods carry a default 300s toleration for that taint before eviction.

core.q: You update a ConfigMap that's consumed via env vars (valueFrom.configMapKeyRef) in a running Deployment. Nothing changes in the running pods. Why?
o: ConfigMaps can't be consumed via env vars, only volumes
Env vars are resolved once at container creation; only a pod restart (e.g. kubectl rollout restart) picks up the new values
The ConfigMap update didn't actually persist to etcd
Env var updates require immutable: true to propagate
core.x: Environment variables from a ConfigMap or Secret are resolved exactly once at container creation; updating the object afterward changes nothing until the pod restarts.

core.q: The same ConfigMap is mounted as a volume, but the container mounts a single key via subPath. Does the file update live when the ConfigMap changes?
o: Yes, subPath mounts always refresh via the ..data symlink swap
Yes, but only after the pod is deleted and recreated
No — subPath mounts copy the file rather than symlink through ..data, so it never sees updates
No, because ConfigMaps are always immutable once mounted
core.x: Normal volume mounts update atomically via a symlink swap through ..data, but subPath mounts copy the file instead, so they never receive live updates.

core.q: Is base64 encoding in a Secret's data field a form of encryption?
o: Yes, base64 provides adequate encryption for etcd-at-rest storage
Yes, but only for Secrets, not ConfigMaps
No, but etcd encrypts Secrets automatically by default with no configuration
No — base64 is encoding, not encryption; real protection requires enabling encryption at rest via an EncryptionConfiguration with a KMS provider
core.x: base64 exists so arbitrary bytes survive JSON transport; by default Secrets sit in etcd as plaintext, so real protection needs encryption at rest via a KMS provider.

core.q: A Deployment references a Secret key via a required env var (valueFrom, no optional: true), but the key doesn't exist. What happens?
o: The container fails to start with CreateContainerConfigError
The container starts with an empty string for that variable
The Pod is stuck ContainerCreating with mount errors in Events
The API server rejects the Pod at admission time
core.x: A required env-var reference to a missing key blocks the container from starting with CreateContainerConfigError; a missing volume-referenced object instead leaves the Pod stuck ContainerCreating with mount errors.

core.q: Why does setting immutable: true on a ConfigMap reduce load on the API server at scale?
o: It compresses the ConfigMap's data before storage
The kubelet stops opening a watch for it, removing per-node watch load across the cluster
It moves the ConfigMap's storage from etcd to tmpfs
It disables RBAC checks on the object
core.x: immutable: true both blocks further edits and stops kubelets from watching the object, which removes significant watch load in clusters with tens of thousands of pods.

core.q: Your Ingress controller needs a TLS secret, but a teammate's kubectl create secret generic produced type Opaque. What breaks, and why?
o: Nothing breaks — Ingress controllers accept any Secret type
The Secret is auto-converted to kubernetes.io/tls on first use
Ingress controllers require type kubernetes.io/tls specifically, which mandates tls.crt and tls.key keys; an Opaque secret won't be accepted
The Pod using the Ingress fails RBAC checks
core.x: Secret types are validation contracts consumers key off of — Ingress controllers specifically demand type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt and tls.key.

core.q:
$ kubectl get nodes
NAME     STATUS     ROLES           AGE   VERSION
cp-1     Ready      control-plane   90d   v1.31.2
node-1   Ready      <none>          90d   v1.31.2
node-2   NotReady   <none>          90d   v1.31.2

$ kubectl describe node node-2 | grep -A2 Taints
Taints: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute
        node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoSchedule

What happened to node-2, and what happens to pods running on it?
o: node-2's api-server crashed; pods on it are immediately deleted
node-2 lost etcd quorum; the cluster is now read-only
The scheduler marked node-2 unschedulable via kubectl cordon; running pods stay untouched

node-2's kubelet stopped heartbeating, the node controller marked it NotReady and tainted it; pods get evicted after the default 300s toleration expires, though original containers may still be running on the cut-off node
core.x: A missed heartbeat leads the node controller to mark the node NotReady and apply the unreachable:NoExecute taint; replacement pods appear elsewhere after the 300s toleration, but the original containers may still be alive on the partitioned node.

core.q: The kube-apiserver goes down entirely but etcd, kubelet, and kube-proxy are healthy. What still works, and what doesn't?
o: Existing pods keep running and Services keep routing traffic via existing kube-proxy rules; but no kubectl commands, new pods, scaling, or rescheduling can happen
Nothing works at all — the whole cluster stops serving traffic
New pods can still be scheduled since the scheduler talks to etcd directly
Only DNS resolution breaks; everything else continues normally
core.x: The api-server is the only component with an etcd connection; when it's down the data plane runs on autopilot but nothing can change, since the scheduler and controllers only ever talk through the api-server.

core.q: Your 5-node etcd cluster loses 3 members simultaneously. What happens to the cluster?
o: It keeps operating normally since 2 members remain online
It loses quorum (needs a majority of 5, i.e. 3) and refuses all writes and consistent reads — the cluster freezes at its last committed state
etcd automatically re-elects a leader from the remaining 2 and continues writes
Only read operations are affected; writes continue via the surviving members
core.x: etcd is a Raft cluster requiring a strict majority to commit writes; with only 2 of 5 members left, quorum is lost and the cluster freezes until a majority returns.

core.q: New pods from a rollout and a scale-up are stuck Pending, with zero FailedScheduling events, while already-running pods are unaffected. Which control-plane component is most likely down?
o: kube-controller-manager
kubelet on the affected nodes
kube-scheduler
etcd
core.x: New pods piling up in Pending with no scheduling events (and existing workloads unaffected) is the canonical signature of the scheduler itself being down.

core.q: You delete a Deployment's pod manually while kube-controller-manager is down. What happens?
o: The ReplicaSet controller creates a replacement pod after a short delay
The scheduler recreates the pod directly, bypassing the ReplicaSet controller
The api-server refuses the deletion since no controller is available
No replacement pod appears — the reconciliation loop that would recreate it isn't running
core.x: kube-controller-manager hosts the ReplicaSet controller's reconciliation loop; without it, the API accepts the deletion but nothing acts to restore the desired replica count.

core.q: You can curl a Service's ClusterIP successfully but curl my-svc.my-ns.svc.cluster.local fails to resolve. What's the most likely cause?
o: CoreDNS is down or misbehaving — DNS-based service discovery fails while raw IP routing (via existing kube-proxy rules) still works
kube-proxy has crashed on every node
The api-server is down
etcd lost quorum
core.x: CoreDNS is an addon Deployment, not a control-plane binary, but its failure mimics a total outage for name-based traffic while ClusterIP routing (kube-proxy's job) keeps working — the discriminating test interviewers like.

core.q: A ClusterRole named 'view' is bound to a ServiceAccount via a RoleBinding in namespace 'dev' only. Can that ServiceAccount list pods in namespace 'prod'?
o: Yes, because ClusterRoles always grant cluster-wide access regardless of binding type
No — a namespaced RoleBinding referencing a ClusterRole grants those rules only within the binding's own namespace
Yes, but only for read verbs like list and get
No, because ClusterRoles cannot be referenced by RoleBindings at all
core.x: The binding's scope wins: a ClusterRole referenced by a namespaced RoleBinding grants that ClusterRole's rules only within the binding's namespace, not cluster-wide.
core.t: The classic trap is assuming ClusterRole always means cluster-wide — it's the binding type that decides scope.

core.q: A teammate wants to change an existing RoleBinding to point at a different ClusterRole by editing roleRef in place. Does this work?
o: Yes, roleRef can be patched freely at any time
Yes, but only for ClusterRoleBindings, not RoleBindings
No — roleRef is immutable after creation; you must delete and recreate the binding (or use kubectl auth reconcile)
No, RoleBindings themselves are entirely immutable, including subjects
core.x: roleRef is deliberately immutable so an existing grant can't be silently repurposed; changing it requires deleting and recreating the binding.

core.q: The API server returns: 'User system:serviceaccount:dev:app-sa cannot list resource "deployments" in API group "apps" in the namespace "prod"'. What's the correct first thing to check?
o: Whether the ServiceAccount's token has expired
Whether the api-server certificate is valid
Whether etcd has quorum
Whether there is a binding for that subject in the 'prod' namespace specifically, since RoleBindings don't cross namespaces
core.x: Decoding a 403 starts with checking for a binding for that exact subject in the exact namespace named in the error, since RoleBindings never cross namespace boundaries.

core.q: What's the difference between a 401 and a 403 response from the API server?
o: 401 means authentication failed (bad/expired token or cert); 403 means authentication succeeded but RBAC denied the action
401 means RBAC denied the action; 403 means authentication failed
Both mean the same thing — RBAC denial — just at different API versions
401 only occurs for ServiceAccounts; 403 only occurs for human users
core.x: 401 is an authentication failure (identity unknown), while 403 means authentication succeeded but authorization was denied — conflating them sends you debugging the wrong layer.

core.q: A developer with rights to create pods in namespace 'dev' insists they have no way to read Secrets there since they were never granted 'get secrets'. Is this reasoning sound?
o: Yes — pod-create rights and secret-read rights are completely independent
No — anyone who can create pods can mount any secret in that namespace into their pod, making pod-create rights secret-read rights in disguise
Yes, unless they also have the 'impersonate' verb
No, but only if automountServiceAccountToken is true
core.x: A subject who can create pods can mount any secret in that namespace into a pod they control and read it that way, so pod-create rights are effectively secret-read rights.

core.q: Why do modern ServiceAccount tokens (from the TokenRequest API) improve on legacy service-account-token Secrets?
o: They are stored permanently in etcd for auditability
They grant cluster-admin by default for easier debugging
They are audience-bound, pod-bound (invalid once the pod dies), and time-limited (~1h, auto-refreshed), unlike legacy tokens which never expired
They eliminate the need for RBAC entirely
core.x: Projected TokenRequest tokens are scoped, short-lived, and tied to the pod's lifetime, unlike legacy service-account-token Secrets which never expired and sat readable in etcd.

core.q: A teammate installs a CRD for PostgresCluster but no controller is deployed yet. They create a PostgresCluster object. What happens?
o: The api-server rejects the object since no controller is registered
A default StatefulSet is automatically created for it
The object is stored but immediately marked Terminating until a controller appears
The object is validated and stored in etcd like any resource, but nothing happens in the world — there's no behavior without a controller
core.x: A CRD alone is schema registration; the api-server serves full CRUD for it, but without a controller reconciling it, creating an object changes nothing in the world.

core.q:
$ kubectl get postgrescluster main-db -o yaml
spec:
  replicas: 3
  version: "16"
status:
  readyReplicas: 1
  conditions:
  - type: Progressing
    status: "True"
    reason: CreatingReplica
What does the mismatch between spec.replicas and status.readyReplicas tell you, and who is allowed to write each field?
o: spec is the desired state (user-writable) and status is the observed state (controller-writable only); here the controller has achieved 1 of the 3 desired replicas and is still working
Both fields are user-writable; the mismatch means a validation webhook failed
status.readyReplicas is set by the scheduler, not the controller
The mismatch indicates the CRD schema is misconfigured
core.x: The spec/status split is a write-ownership contract — users write spec (desired), only the controller writes status (observed) — so this mismatch simply shows reconciliation still in progress.

core.q: A namespace is stuck in Terminating state indefinitely after deletion. What is the most likely cause?
o: The api-server is down
Some controller responsible for removing its finalizer is dead or erroring, so the finalizer list never empties and deletion never completes
etcd lost quorum during the deletion
The namespace has a NoExecute taint applied
core.x: While finalizers are non-empty, deletion only sets deletionTimestamp and the object persists Terminating; a dead or erroring controller that never removes its finalizer is THE cause of stuck-Terminating objects.

core.q: Why does deleting a CRD potentially wipe out related cloud resources (e.g. real databases an operator provisioned)?
o: Deleting a CRD only removes the schema, never the custom resource instances
It doesn't — CRDs and their instances are fully independent of any cleanup logic
Deleting a CRD deletes every instance of that custom resource cluster-wide, and via the operator's own finalizer-driven cleanup this can cascade to deprovisioning real external resources
Cloud resources are only affected if RBAC grants the 'escalate' verb
core.x: Deleting a CRD deletes every instance of that resource cluster-wide, and if the operator's cleanup logic runs on that deletion, real external resources can be torn down too — which is why Helm deliberately leaves CRDs behind on uninstall.

core.q: How do controllers avoid hammering the API server while tracking thousands of objects?
o: They poll the API in a tight loop with rate limiting
They cache objects in etcd directly, bypassing the api-server
They subscribe to a Kafka-like event log maintained by etcd
They use informers — a client-side watch plus in-memory cache feeding a deduplicating workqueue that worker goroutines reconcile
core.x: Informers maintain a watch-fed local cache and enqueue object keys onto a deduplicating workqueue, letting a single controller pod track thousands of objects without polling the api-server.

core.q: Two different controller instances both try to update the same custom resource's status at nearly the same time. How is the conflict resolved?
o: Optimistic concurrency via resourceVersion causes the stale write to fail with a 409 Conflict, which the workqueue simply retries against the fresher object
The api-server queues writes and applies them sequentially with no errors
A distributed lock service external to Kubernetes must be used
The first writer wins permanently and the second write is silently dropped
core.x: Reconcilers rely on resourceVersion-based optimistic concurrency; a stale write fails with 409 Conflict and the workqueue retries it against the current object, no locking required.

netstore.q: Your Deployment shows 3/3 pods Running, but curl to the Service ClusterIP times out. What should you check first?
o: kubectl get endpointslices for the Service — readiness probes may be failing
Restart the pods
Delete and recreate the Service
Check the node's kubelet logs
netstore.x: Running pods can still have failing readiness probes, which keeps them out of EndpointSlices (ready:true). A Service with no ready endpoints times out even though pods look healthy in kubectl get pods.

netstore.q: A teammate says 'ping 10.96.4.7 fails but curl 10.96.4.7:80 works, so the Service must be broken.' Why is this reasoning wrong?
o: The ClusterIP only supports UDP, not ICMP or TCP
ping requires root privileges inside the pod
ClusterIP is a virtual IP enforced only by iptables/IPVS DNAT rules; ICMP has no rewrite rule so ping fails, while the TCP connection is correctly DNAT'd
The Service is in fact broken and curl succeeded by coincidence
netstore.x: No process listens on the ClusterIP anywhere — it's kernel rules programmed by kube-proxy. TCP connections get DNAT'd to a ready pod; ICMP has no such rule, so ping failing is expected, not a sign of breakage.

netstore.q: In a Service manifest, what is the difference between port and targetPort?
o: They must always be equal
port is what the Service listens on at the ClusterIP; targetPort is the container port traffic is DNAT'd to
targetPort is only used for NodePort services
port is randomly assigned by kube-proxy
netstore.x: port is the ClusterIP-facing port clients dial (e.g. 80); targetPort is where DNAT lands on the pod (e.g. 8080), and can be a named port so different pods use different container ports.

netstore.q: 500 office users share a single egress NAT IP and hit a Service with sessionAffinity: ClientIP. What incident pattern is likely?
o: Even load balancing across all pods
The Service silently ignores sessionAffinity behind NAT
DNS round-robin overrides the affinity setting
All 500 users stick to a single backend pod for up to 3 hours, leaving other pods idle
netstore.x: ClientIP affinity uses conntrack keyed on source IP with a default 10800s (3h) timeout. Behind NAT, many real users share one source IP, so they all stick to the same pod — a classic 'one pod hot, rest idle' incident.

netstore.q: Why does a headless Service (clusterIP: None) exist, and what does it change about DNS?
o: It disables DNS entirely for that Service
It forces all traffic through NodePort
It is only valid for LoadBalancer type Services
It skips the virtual IP; DNS returns individual pod IPs as multiple A records instead of one VIP, letting clients pick a specific replica
netstore.x: Headless Services program no kube-proxy rules; cluster DNS instead returns one A record per ready pod IP, which StatefulSets rely on for stable per-pod names like mysql-0.mysql.db.svc.cluster.local.

netstore.q:
You run: kubectl describe svc web

Endpoints: <none>

kubectl get pods shows the backing Deployment's 3 pods as Running. What are the two most likely causes?
o: The Service type is wrong, or the node is out of disk
Selector label mismatch between the Service and the pods, or the pods are failing their readiness probes
The ClusterIP CIDR is exhausted
CoreDNS is down
netstore.x: An empty Endpoints/EndpointSlice with Running pods points to either a selector/label typo (app: web vs app: webapp) or readiness probes failing, since only ready:true pods populate endpoints.
netstore.h: Recall the trap described for the services card: check endpoints, not pod status.

netstore.q: Why does IPVS mode scale better than iptables mode for kube-proxy in clusters with 5,000+ Services?
o: IPVS runs entirely in userspace and skips the kernel
iptables mode does not support TCP
IPVS uses an in-kernel hash table with real scheduling algorithms instead of evaluating thousands of sequential iptables rules
IPVS eliminates the need for EndpointSlices
netstore.x: iptables mode evaluates rules sequentially; IPVS uses an in-kernel hash table with algorithms like rr, lc, sh, which scales far better at high Service counts.

netstore.q: What is the key behavioral difference between externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster and externalTrafficPolicy: Local for a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service?
o: Cluster mode SNATs traffic (client IP is hidden) and forwards to any node; Local mode preserves the client source IP but drops traffic on nodes with no local backend pod
Cluster mode is IPv6-only
Local mode disables health checks entirely
There is no functional difference, only a naming difference
netstore.x: Cluster mode forwards to any node and SNATs, hiding the real client IP from pods. Local mode preserves the source IP but nodes without a local endpoint drop the traffic instead of forwarding it; cloud LBs pair this with health-check NodePorts.

netstore.q: A pod in namespace shop runs nslookup payments and it resolves successfully to a ClusterIP, even though the Service is also named payments. How is the short name resolved?
o: CoreDNS guesses the namespace from the pod's labels
kubelet writes a search list in /etc/resolv.conf (shop.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local), so 'payments' is retried as payments.shop.svc.cluster.local
Short names are cached from the last successful lookup
The pod must have a hosts file entry pre-populated
netstore.x: kubelet writes a 3-entry search list into every pod's resolv.conf; a lookup for 'payments' is silently expanded against that list until one succeeds — here, payments.shop.svc.cluster.local.

netstore.q: An app makes frequent calls to an external API, api.stripe.com, and engineers notice spiky latency plus high CoreDNS query volume. What's the likely root cause?
o: The external API is rate-limiting the cluster
CoreDNS caching is disabled by default
The pod's dnsPolicy is set to None
ndots:5 makes api.stripe.com (2 dots) get expanded through the whole search list first, producing three guaranteed NXDOMAIN queries before the real upstream query fires
netstore.x: With ndots:5, any name with fewer than 5 dots is tried against the search list before being sent upstream as-is, so external names like api.stripe.com generate extra NXDOMAIN lookups against CoreDNS — a classic ndots latency gotcha.

netstore.q: A pod is configured with hostNetwork: true and dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst. Service names stop resolving from inside it. Why?
o: For hostNetwork pods, ClusterFirst silently degrades to the node's resolv.conf instead of cluster DNS; ClusterFirstWithHostNet is required to keep cluster DNS
hostNetwork pods can never resolve DNS
The pod needs an explicit nameserver entry in its Service manifest
hostNetwork disables CoreDNS cluster-wide
netstore.x: ClusterFirst silently falls back to the node's own resolv.conf for hostNetwork pods. dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet is the documented fix to keep using cluster DNS in that case.

netstore.q:
You debug with: kubectl exec -it dbg -- nslookup mysql.db.svc.cluster.local

Name: mysql.db.svc.cluster.local
Address: 10.244.1.5
Address: 10.244.2.9
Address: 10.244.3.3

What kind of Service is mysql, and why are there multiple addresses?
o: A LoadBalancer Service with 3 external IPs
A misconfigured Service with duplicate selectors
A headless Service (clusterIP: None) — DNS returns one A record per ready pod IP instead of a single ClusterIP
A NodePort Service exposing 3 ports
netstore.x: A regular Service always resolves to exactly one A record (the ClusterIP). Multiple A records, one per pod, is the signature of a headless Service — load balancing happens at DNS/client level instead of kube-proxy.

netstore.q: A NetworkPolicy egress-isolates a namespace, and afterward all Service name lookups start timing out from pods in it. What's missing?
o: An explicit egress allow rule to kube-system on both UDP and TCP port 53 for CoreDNS
The Service's targetPort is wrong
The pod's dnsPolicy must be set to None
CoreDNS itself must be restarted after every NetworkPolicy change
netstore.x: Cluster DNS relies on egress to CoreDNS in kube-system on port 53. Egress isolation without an explicit DNS allow rule (UDP AND TCP 53) breaks nearly every lookup.

netstore.q: Why does the interview-standard debugging flow start with nslookup kubernetes.default before checking your own app's Service?
o: kubernetes.default is a special DNS record with no dependency on CoreDNS
It restarts CoreDNS as a side effect
kubernetes.default is the only Service guaranteed to always exist, so its failure isolates the problem to CoreDNS/DNS path rather than your app
It bypasses ndots expansion entirely
netstore.x: kubernetes.default always exists on any cluster. If it fails to resolve, the problem is CoreDNS itself or the path to it (crashlooping pods, a NetworkPolicy eating port 53) — not your application.

netstore.q: Which statement about pod DNS records is accurate per the cluster DNS model?
o: Every pod automatically gets a resolvable hostname-based DNS record
Only the IP-based form (10-244-1-5.shop.pod.cluster.local) always works; hostname-based records require spec.hostname + spec.subdomain matching a headless Service
Pods never get any DNS record, only Services do
Pod DNS records are stored in /etc/hosts, not CoreDNS
netstore.x: Plain pod names are NOT resolvable by default — a frequent false assumption. Only the IP-based form always works, and named records need explicit hostname/subdomain configuration tied to a headless Service.

netstore.q: You create an Ingress resource in a fresh cluster with no controller installed. What happens?
o: kube-apiserver rejects the object with a validation error
Kubernetes automatically installs ingress-nginx
Traffic is routed using default kube-proxy rules
Nothing errors and nothing happens — the Ingress is inert YAML until a controller watches and claims it
netstore.x: The Ingress object does nothing by itself. It requires an ingress controller to watch it and program a real proxy; with none installed, creation silently succeeds but has zero effect — the #1 'why doesn't my Ingress work' answer.

netstore.q:
You run:

$ curl http://<lb-ip>/
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

$ curl -H 'Host: shop.example.com' http://<lb-ip>/
HTTP/1.1 200 OK

The Ingress only defines a rule for host: shop.example.com. Why does the first request 404?
o: The backend Service has no ready endpoints
The TLS secret is missing
pathType is set to Exact
Without the right Host header, the request matches no host rule and falls through to the default backend
netstore.x: 404 signals a routing/claiming problem, not a backend problem. Sending no Host header (or the wrong one) matches no host rule, so the controller serves its default 404 backend.

netstore.q: An Ingress rule matches correctly, but clients get a 502/503. What does this indicate versus a 404, and what's the 30-second triage?
o: 404 and 502 mean the same thing: check DNS
A matched rule but a dead upstream — run kubectl describe ingress plus kubectl get endpointslices for the backend Service
502/503 always means the TLS certificate expired
Restart the ingress controller pod immediately
netstore.x: 404 = no rule matched (routing problem). 502/503 = a rule matched but the upstream Service/backend failed (bad Service name/port, no ready endpoints, or connection resets) — describe ingress + get endpointslices is the fast triage.

netstore.q: An Ingress rule uses path: /api with pathType: Prefix. Which incoming request path does NOT match?
o: /api
/api/v1
/apiary
/api/
netstore.x: Prefix matching operates on whole path segments. /api matches /api and /api/v1 (and /api/) but NOT /apiary, since that isn't a segment boundary match.

netstore.q: A browser shows a certificate warning naming 'Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate' when visiting an HTTPS Ingress host. What does this indicate?
o: The Ingress's TLS secret's cert SANs don't cover the requested host, so the controller falls back to its self-signed default certificate
The cluster has no TLS support at all
The client's browser is misconfigured
DNS resolved to the wrong load balancer
netstore.x: When the referenced cert's SANs don't cover the requested host, the controller silently serves its self-signed 'Fake Certificate' — a dead giveaway of a cert/host mismatch, per the card's TLS facts.

netstore.q: Why can one LoadBalancer + one ingress controller front dozens of Services more cost-effectively than Service type: LoadBalancer per Service?
o: Ingress compresses HTTP traffic to reduce bandwidth costs
LoadBalancer Services are L4 and each gets its own cloud LB and IP; Ingress is L7 and shares a single entry point that reads Host/path to route to many backend Services
Ingress controllers run without any load balancer at all
kube-proxy automatically merges multiple LoadBalancer Services into one IP
netstore.x: Service type LoadBalancer is L4 — every Service pays for its own cloud LB and IP, with no URL awareness. Ingress moves routing to L7 behind one shared LB, using Host/path rules to fan out to many Services.

netstore.q: What does the Ingress spec's TLS block require, and what happens if it's missing while a host rule still exists?
o: Nothing — TLS is automatic for all Ingress hosts
The Secret can live in any namespace as long as it's named correctly
TLS termination always happens at the backend pod, never at the controller
A tls block needs a hosts list and a secretName pointing at a kubernetes.io/tls Secret in the SAME namespace; without it, the controller terminates HTTP only for that host, not HTTPS
netstore.x: TLS is declared per-Ingress via hosts + secretName referencing a kubernetes.io/tls Secret in the same namespace as the Ingress; without it there's no HTTPS termination configured for that host.

netstore.q: A team applies a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} and policyTypes: [Ingress], containing zero ingress rules. What's the effect?
o: It default-denies all ingress to every pod in the namespace, since selection alone triggers isolation regardless of rule content
Nothing — an empty rules list means no policy is enforced
It allows all ingress since there are no explicit deny rules
It only affects pods that are also selected by another policy
netstore.x: Isolation is triggered by selection, not rule content. podSelector: {} selects every pod; policyTypes: [Ingress] with no rules isolates them all with nothing allowed in — the canonical default-deny pattern.

netstore.q: In a NetworkPolicy 'from' block, what's the difference between one list entry containing both namespaceSelector and podSelector, versus two separate dashed entries for each?
o: No difference; YAML normalizes both to the same rule
Two separate entries always causes a validation error
One entry with both selectors is an AND (pods matching podSelector INSIDE matching namespaces); two separate entries is an OR (either match qualifies)
namespaceSelector is ignored unless it's in its own entry
netstore.x: This is the classic AND/OR trap: a single from: entry with both selectors means AND; two dashed list entries mean OR. A stray extra '-' silently turns a tight rule into a much looser one — YAML won't warn you.

netstore.q:
You run:

$ kubectl exec -it app -- nc -zv -w2 db 5432
nc: db (10.96.14.2:5432): Operation timed out

$ kubectl exec -it dbg -- nc -zv -w2 10.244.3.9 5432
Connection to 10.244.3.9 5432 port [tcp/*] succeeded!

(dbg is not selected by any NetworkPolicy; app is.) What does this timeout-vs-success pattern suggest?
o: A NetworkPolicy is silently dropping the packets — timeouts point at policy or firewall drops, not a listening problem
The database process has crashed
The DB Service's targetPort is misconfigured
DNS is returning a stale ClusterIP
netstore.x: Policy-dropped packets are silently discarded, producing client timeouts, not refused connections. 'Refused' would mean reaching the host with nothing listening (ports/endpoints issue). Timeout + working connectivity from an unselected pod is the classic NetworkPolicy signature.

netstore.q: A team applies default-deny-egress to a namespace, then immediately applies default-deny-ingress, planning to add the DNS-allow rule last. What breaks, and why does ordering matter?
o: Nothing breaks; order is irrelevant since policies are additive
Ingress rules take priority over egress rules automatically
The whole namespace loses name resolution immediately, because egress to CoreDNS on port 53 wasn't allowed before egress was locked down
The API server rejects policies applied out of order
netstore.x: The documented rollout order is: label namespaces, allow DNS egress everywhere, THEN default-deny ingress, THEN default-deny egress. Reversing that (deny egress before allowing DNS) takes down name resolution for the whole namespace in one apply.

netstore.q: A NetworkPolicy tries to restrict traffic 'to the database Service' using an ipBlock with the Service's ClusterIP CIDR. Why is this unreliable?
o: ipBlock only supports IPv6 addresses
Policies select pods, not Services — kube-proxy DNATs Service traffic to a pod IP BEFORE policy evaluation, so ipBlock on a ClusterIP CIDR doesn't reliably match
ClusterIPs are randomly reassigned every few minutes
ipBlock cannot be combined with podSelector in the same policy
netstore.x: Policies evaluate against pod IPs, since kube-proxy has already DNAT'd Service traffic before policy enforcement. ipBlock is meant for real external CIDRs; matching pod traffic via a ClusterIP CIDR is explicitly unreliable.

netstore.q: Pod A successfully opens a TCP connection to Pod B under a restrictive NetworkPolicy setup. Do you also need a mirrored ingress rule on A to allow B's replies back?
o: Yes, every egress rule needs a matching ingress rule on the initiator
Only if the connection uses UDP instead of TCP
Only if sessionAffinity: ClientIP is set on the Service
No — connection tracking allows reply packets automatically once the initiating connection is permitted; policies govern connection initiation, not both directions
netstore.x: Reply packets are handled by conntrack: if the initial connection was allowed, responses flow back automatically. You do not write a mirror rule for the reverse direction of an established flow.

netstore.q: A cluster runs classic Flannel as its CNI. The team applies several NetworkPolicies and traffic is still unrestricted. What's the likely explanation?
o: NetworkPolicy YAML syntax is invalid
NetworkPolicies require a paid Kubernetes distribution
The policies need a namespace label to activate
Flannel (classic) doesn't implement NetworkPolicy enforcement, so policies are accepted by the API but silently ignored
netstore.x: NetworkPolicy enforcement is the CNI's job. Calico and Cilium enforce it; classic Flannel does not — an unenforced policy fails silently, a documented operational trap.

netstore.q: A policy needs to allow ingress from 'the monitoring namespace'. What must be true for namespaceSelector: matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring} to work?
o: The monitoring namespace must be manually labeled 'name: monitoring' first
Nothing extra — this label is automatically applied to every namespace by its name
namespaceSelector only matches namespace names directly, labels are irrelevant
This selector syntax is invalid and must use podSelector instead
netstore.x: namespaceSelector matches namespace LABELS, not raw names. Every namespace automatically carries kubernetes.io/metadata.name: <name>, making matchLabels on that key the modern, label-hygiene-free way to select a namespace by name.

netstore.q:
kubectl describe pod on a stuck pod shows:

Warning  FailedCreatePodSandBox  kubelet  Failed to create pod
sandbox: plugin type="calico" failed: error adding container to
network: no configuration found in /etc/cni/net.d

Meanwhile pods that were already running on that node keep serving traffic fine. What does this split symptom indicate?
o: A total node network outage affecting all traffic
The pod's application code has a bug
A CNI failure on that node — new pods can't get sandboxes created, but already-running pods keep working because their veths/routes were wired before the failure
The Service's selector no longer matches
netstore.x: CNI plugins are invoked at sandbox creation. A broken CNI stops NEW pods at ContainerCreating while already-running pods keep working since their networking was already wired — the classic CNI-outage fingerprint, distinct from a total network outage.

netstore.q: A node shows NotReady with 'container runtime network not ready: NetworkReady=false ... cni plugin not initialized'. What is the standard triage pair?
o: Check /etc/cni/net.d/ for config presence and confirm the CNI DaemonSet pod is actually Running on that node
Restart kubelet and hope it self-heals
Reboot the node immediately
Increase the node's pod CIDR size
netstore.x: This exact message means kubelet found no CNI config in /etc/cni/net.d/. The documented triage is: config present in /etc/cni/net.d/, binaries present in /opt/cni/bin/, and is the CNI DaemonSet pod Running on that node.

netstore.q: Requests with small payloads succeed between pods on different nodes, but large-payload requests hang or fail intermittently. What CNI-layer explanation fits?
o: The Service's sessionAffinity is misconfigured
A VXLAN overlay's encapsulation reduces the effective MTU; mismatched MTU causes large packets to fail while small ones succeed
The pod CIDR has been exhausted
CoreDNS is returning stale records
netstore.x: VXLAN overlays wrap pod packets in UDP, reducing effective MTU. A mismatched MTU produces the infamous 'small requests work, large payloads hang' bug — a classic overlay networking gotcha.

netstore.q: What core guarantee does the Kubernetes network model require that a CNI plugin must implement?
o: Every pod shares the node's IP for simplicity
Pods must NAT all cross-node traffic through kube-proxy
Only pods in the same namespace can communicate
Every pod gets its own IP, and all pods can reach all other pods across nodes WITHOUT NAT
netstore.x: The contract is: every pod gets a real IP, all pods reach all pods across nodes without NAT, node agents can reach node pods, and a pod sees itself at the same IP others see. CNI plugins implement this; Kubernetes itself does not.

netstore.q: A pod fails to schedule with the event 'failed to allocate for range: no IP addresses available', while the node otherwise looks healthy. What's the likely cause?
o: The node's pod CIDR slice (e.g. a /24, ~250 IPs) is exhausted, capping how many pods that node can host
The node's kubelet certificate has expired
The Service CIDR has been exhausted
The container runtime is out of disk space
netstore.x: Each node typically owns a pod CIDR slice from the cluster CIDR; a /24 caps it at roughly 250 usable pod IPs. Exhausting that range produces exactly this 'no IP addresses available' event while the node itself looks otherwise healthy.

netstore.q: Why can DaemonSets like the CNI plugin itself start scheduling on a node that is still NotReady?
o: DaemonSets ignore node readiness entirely for all pods, always
NotReady nodes automatically become Ready once any pod is scheduled
DaemonSets with the right tolerations bypass the NotReady gate, which is the bootstrap trick that lets the CNI's own DaemonSet bring networking up
kubelet grants an exception only to pods running as root
netstore.x: kubelet's Ready condition gates most workloads from scheduling, but DaemonSets with appropriate tolerations can still be placed — this is exactly how the CNI's own DaemonSet gets onto a NotReady node to bring up networking in the first place.

netstore.q: How does Cilium's eBPF datapath change kube-proxy-style Service handling compared to iptables mode, according to the card?
o: It replaces iptables chains with in-kernel eBPF programs, so Service resolution and policy checks don't degrade as O(rules) with thousands of Services, and can fully replace kube-proxy
It requires more iptables rules for large clusters
It moves all networking into userspace for easier debugging
It disables NetworkPolicy enforcement to gain speed
netstore.x: eBPF programs attached in the kernel avoid the O(rules) degradation of sequential iptables chains, letting large clusters scale Service/policy handling — this is the documented reason large clusters move off iptables-mode kube-proxy.

netstore.q: A PVC requesting ReadWriteOnce is already mounted read-write by a pod on node1. A second pod is scheduled onto node1 as well and also mounts it read-write. A third pod is scheduled onto node2 and tries to mount the same PVC. What happens?
o: All three pods mount successfully since RWO allows unlimited pods
Only one pod total may ever mount an RWO volume
The first two pods (both on node1) succeed; the third pod on node2 fails to attach with a Multi-Attach error, because RWO counts NODES, not pods
The PVC automatically converts to RWX to accommodate the third pod
netstore.x: ReadWriteOnce means one NODE can mount read-write. Multiple pods on that same node can all write; a pod on a different node fails with 'Multi-Attach error for volume' — the single most-missed access-mode distinction.

netstore.q:
You run:

$ kubectl describe pvc data
Status: Pending
Events:
  Type    Reason                Message
  ----    ------                -------
  Normal  WaitForFirstConsumer  waiting for first consumer to be
                                 created before binding

What should you do?
o: Treat it as an error and delete/recreate the PVC
Nothing is wrong — this is WaitForFirstConsumer working as designed; create the pod that will use the claim
Manually patch the PV's claimRef to force binding
Switch the StorageClass's reclaimPolicy to Delete
netstore.x: This message is normal, not an error, when volumeBindingMode is WaitForFirstConsumer — provisioning is deliberately delayed until a pod actually consumes the claim so the scheduler can pick the node/zone first.

netstore.q: A team deletes a PVC bound to a PV with reclaimPolicy: Retain, expecting to recreate the PVC and reattach seamlessly. Instead, the new PVC stays Pending and the old PV shows status Released. Why?
o: Retain automatically wipes the disk, so there's nothing left to bind
PVs can never be reused once a PVC is deleted, regardless of reclaimPolicy
The new PVC must use a different StorageClass to bind to a Released PV
The PV's spec.claimRef still points at the deleted claim's UID; it must be manually cleared (patched/edited) before the PV becomes Available again
netstore.x: Retain preserves both the PV object and its data, but the dangling claimRef prevents automatic re-binding. Recovery requires deliberately patching/editing the PV to clear claimRef, exposing the data to the next claimant.

netstore.q: A cluster has no default StorageClass, and a PVC is created without setting storageClassName at all. What happens?
o: The PVC binds to any available PV regardless of class
Kubernetes creates a default StorageClass automatically
The PVC is rejected at creation time by the API server
The PVC stays Pending forever with an event like 'no persistent volumes available for this claim and no storage class is set'
netstore.x: Omitting storageClassName normally gets mutated to the default class — but with no default class configured, and no matching static PV, the PVC sits Pending eternally. This is called out as the #1 storage question on fresh clusters.

netstore.q: What is the practical difference between a PVC with storageClassName: "" (empty string) versus one that simply omits storageClassName?
o: They are functionally identical in all cases
Empty string explicitly opts OUT of dynamic provisioning and matches only classless static PVs; omitting the field lets it be mutated to the cluster's default class if one exists
Omitting the field always fails validation
Empty string forces the PVC to use the fast-ssd class by convention
netstore.x: storageClassName: "" is a deliberate statement to skip dynamic provisioning entirely, matching only pre-existing classless static PVs — a different behavior from simply omitting the field, which defers to the default class.

netstore.q: A pod using a dynamically provisioned PVC fails to schedule with the event 'volume node affinity conflict'. What's the likely root cause?
o: The PVC's access mode is incompatible with the StorageClass
The reclaimPolicy is set to Retain instead of Delete
volumeBindingMode: Immediate provisioned the disk in one zone before the pod's node affinity forced scheduling into a different zone, since cloud block volumes are zonal
CoreDNS cannot resolve the storage provisioner's Service
netstore.x: Immediate binding mode can provision in a zone that later conflicts with where the pod's node affinity/scheduling constraints require it to land, since block volumes are zonal. WaitForFirstConsumer exists specifically to avoid this by delaying provisioning until after pod placement.

netstore.q: A StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: true, and a team wants to shrink an over-provisioned 100Gi PVC down to 20Gi by editing spec.resources.requests.storage. What happens?
o: There is no shrink path — downsizing requires creating a new smaller volume and copying data over; only expansion is supported
The CSI driver shrinks the disk and reclaims the freed space automatically
Shrinking works instantly but destroys existing data
The PVC is automatically deleted and a smaller one is created in its place
netstore.x: Expansion is one-directional: allowVolumeExpansion lets you grow a PVC upward via the CSI driver, but there is no shrink path at all. Downsizing means provisioning a new smaller volume and copying data.

netstore.q:
You run:

$ kubectl get pvc data
NAME   STATUS        VOLUME    CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES
data   Terminating   pvc-abc1  10Gi       RWO

This persists for several minutes after kubectl delete pvc data, and a pod is still mounting it. What's the most likely explanation?
o: The PVC was never actually deleted due to an API server bug
The kubernetes.io/pvc-protection finalizer holds it in Terminating until the last pod actively using it is gone
Terminating PVCs always require manual finalizer removal, even in normal operation
The StorageClass's reclaimPolicy is set to Retain, which blocks all deletion
netstore.x: PVCs (and PVs) in active use are shielded by pvc-protection / pv-protection finalizers. A deleted-but-mounted PVC hangs in Terminating until the last consuming pod is gone — this is expected behavior, not a bug.

troubleshoot.q:
A prod pod shows this:
$ kubectl describe pod payment-api-7d9f8b6c5-x2kqj
State:          Waiting
  Reason:       CrashLoopBackOff
Last State:     Terminated
  Reason:       Error
  Exit Code:    1
Restart Count:  7
Events:
  Warning  BackOff  2m (x21 over 9m)  kubelet  Back-off restarting failed container
What is the single next command to find out why it's dying?
o: kubectl logs payment-api-7d9f8b6c5-x2kqj --previous
kubectl delete pod payment-api-7d9f8b6c5-x2kqj to force a fresh restart
kubectl logs payment-api-7d9f8b6c5-x2kqj (without --previous)
kubectl exec -it payment-api-7d9f8b6c5-x2kqj -- /bin/sh
troubleshoot.x: The container already crashed and restarted; --previous fetches logs from the terminated instance that actually died, while plain logs would show the fresh container that hasn't failed yet.
troubleshoot.h: The current container hasn't failed yet — you need the last one's logs.

troubleshoot.q: Running `kubectl logs mypod` on a CrashLoopBackOff pod returns nothing. What should you conclude?
o: The application never writes to stdout, so you must exec into the container instead
Nothing conclusive yet — the current container is fresh; add --previous to see the crashed instance's logs
The pod's logs were garbage collected after one hour
There genuinely are no logs, so the problem must be a scheduling issue
troubleshoot.x: This is the classic trap: interviewers deliberately set it because forgetting --previous instantly reveals who hasn't debugged a real crash loop.

troubleshoot.q: Three pods are unhealthy but you don't yet know if it's one app, one node, or the whole cluster. What's the fastest way to narrow the investigation before diving into any single pod?
o: Restart all affected pods and see which ones come back healthy
Escalate directly to the platform team without further investigation
Determine the blast radius first — is it one pod, one node, one namespace, or the whole cluster
Immediately run kubectl logs --previous on every pod in the cluster
troubleshoot.x: One question halves the search space: one pod means an app problem, one node means a node problem, everything means control plane/CNI/DNS.

troubleshoot.q: During a live incident where a bad deploy is causing errors, what should you do FIRST?
o: Delete the broken Deployment entirely to stop the errors
Wait until you have the exact exit code before taking any action
Immediately kubectl describe every pod to build a full root-cause picture before touching anything
Mitigate immediately — e.g. kubectl rollout undo — then investigate the broken state calmly afterward
troubleshoot.x: Mitigate-before-root-cause: your first duty in an incident is stopping user impact, not explaining it.

troubleshoot.q: Why is `kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp` preferred over plain `kubectl get events`?
o: Without --sort-by, the event ordering is not guaranteed to be chronological
--sort-by is required to see events across all namespaces
Plain kubectl get events only shows events from the last 60 seconds
Plain kubectl get events omits Warning-type events by default
troubleshoot.x: The flag turns the raw event stream into a readable, genuinely chronological timeline.

troubleshoot.q: You're investigating an incident that started two hours ago, but `kubectl get events` shows nothing relevant to the original failure. Why, and what should you check instead?
o: Events are namespaced, so you simply forgot the -A flag
Events are garbage-collected after about an hour; check restart counts, container Last State, and monitoring history instead
The cluster's audit log has been disabled and needs to be re-enabled
kubectl get events only ever shows the single most recent event per object
troubleshoot.x: Events are ephemeral (~1 hour retention by default), which is exactly why interviewers ask what to do when they're already gone.

troubleshoot.q: A production container image is distroless (no shell), so `kubectl exec -it mypod -- /bin/sh` fails with 'no such file or directory'. What's the documented way to get tooling inside the running pod's namespaces?
o: kubectl exec -it mypod -- /bin/busybox sh
Rebuild and redeploy the image with a shell added, then exec in
kubectl debug -it mypod --image=busybox --target=<container>
kubectl cp busybox:/bin/sh mypod:/bin/sh
troubleshoot.x: Ephemeral debug containers inject real tools into the running pod's namespaces; --target additionally shares the process namespace.

troubleshoot.q: A pod crashes within ~100ms of starting, too fast to `kubectl exec` into. What technique lets you inspect the exact same filesystem, env vars, and mounts at leisure?
o: Increase the container's terminationGracePeriodSeconds to give more time to exec in
kubectl rollout restart and hope to exec in during a slower startup
kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox
kubectl debug <pod> -it --copy-to=dbg --set-image='*=ubuntu' -- sleep 1d
troubleshoot.x: --copy-to creates a disposable clone with the entrypoint overridden so it stays up, sharing the original's filesystem, env vars, and mounts.

troubleshoot.q: In `kubectl describe pod` output, what's the practical difference between seeing a FailedScheduling event versus a BackOff event?
o: FailedScheduling means the pod never reached a node; BackOff means it reached a node and is dying there — two different investigations
FailedScheduling only happens for DaemonSets; BackOff only happens for Deployments
BackOff always means a node problem, while FailedScheduling always means an application bug
They mean the same thing, just from different Kubernetes versions
troubleshoot.x: One screen answers which investigation family you're in.

troubleshoot.q: What are the three commands that make up the core observation trio for Kubernetes triage?
o: kubectl get all, kubectl apply --dry-run, kubectl rollout status
kubectl describe pod, kubectl logs --previous, kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl top pod, kubectl get pod -w, kubectl exec -it
kubectl cluster-info, kubectl version, kubectl config view
troubleshoot.x: describe pod shows state/events, logs --previous shows the dying words, get events gives the cluster timeline.

troubleshoot.q:
Given:
$ kubectl logs payment-api-7d9f8b6c5-x2kqj --previous
FATAL: could not connect to database "payments" at db-primary:5432: connection refused
What does this tell you about where to look next?
o: The container image is corrupted and must be rebuilt
This is definitely an OOMKilled event, so raise the memory limit
The app itself is fine; investigate why db-primary:5432 is unreachable (network, DNS, or the database being down)
The Service selector doesn't match any pod labels
troubleshoot.x: The previous instance's logs name the actual fatal error — a downstream connection failure, not an app bug.

troubleshoot.q: A pod has multiple containers (or init containers) and `kubectl logs mypod` errors out asking you to specify a container. What's the fix?
o: kubectl describe pod always substitutes for logs in multi-container pods
Delete and recreate the pod with only one container
kubectl logs mypod --all-containers is required and has no shorthand
kubectl logs mypod -c <container-name>
troubleshoot.x: The -c flag targets logs at a specific container in a multi-container or init-container pod.

troubleshoot.q: What does `kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml` give you that `kubectl describe pod` might leave ambiguous?
o: The full ground truth stored by the API server — status.conditions and exact containerStatuses including exit codes and image IDs
A live stream of the pod's stdout/stderr
The scheduler's internal decision-making logs
A diff against the previous revision of the pod
troubleshoot.x: -o yaml exposes exactly what the cluster stored, useful for spotting things like an unexpected pulled image digest.

troubleshoot.q: Why does interview-style Kubernetes troubleshooting reward saying the diagnostic loop out loud ('first I'd describe the pod because...') rather than just naming the eventual fix?
o: kubectl commands cannot be run silently in a real interview
It demonstrates a disciplined observe-hypothesize-test loop rather than guessing at fixes, which is what's actually being graded
The fix is usually irrelevant and only command syntax matters
Kubernetes certification exams require verbal explanations
troubleshoot.x: Interviewers are method-testing: observe, hypothesize one cause, test with one command, repeat.

troubleshoot.q:
Given:
$ kubectl get pods -n prod
NAME                    READY STATUS   RESTARTS AGE
checkout-6f7d9c-b2xkq   0/1   Pending  0        12m
$ kubectl describe pod checkout-6f7d9c-b2xkq | tail -3
  Warning FailedScheduling 45s (x9 over 12m) default-scheduler
  0/6 nodes are available: 4 Insufficient memory,
  2 node(s) had untolerated taint {dedicated: gpu}.
What is the diagnosis?
o: The application is crashing on startup due to an out-of-memory condition
The image failed to pull because of a registry authentication error
The scheduler can't place the pod: 4 nodes lack sufficient memory and 2 have an untolerated taint — a scheduling problem, not an app problem
The pod is stuck Terminating because of a finalizer
troubleshoot.x: FailedScheduling itemizes the rejection per node; this pod never reached a node at all.

troubleshoot.q: A junior engineer sees a Pending pod and runs `kubectl logs` on it to investigate. Why is this the wrong move?
o: kubectl logs always requires the -f flag for Pending pods
kubectl logs only works on pods in the Running phase for security reasons
Pending pods delete their logs automatically
A Pending pod hasn't been bound to a node yet, so no container has started and there are no application logs to see
troubleshoot.x: Pending is purely a scheduling conversation; application logs simply don't exist yet.

troubleshoot.q: What are the real Pod phases in Kubernetes (as opposed to the display strings kubectl shows, like CrashLoopBackOff)?
o: Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown
ImagePullBackOff, ContainerCreating, Running, Evicted, Completed
Waiting, Running, Terminated, Ready, NotReady
Pending, Scheduled, Running, CrashLoopBackOff, Terminated
troubleshoot.x: CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, and Terminating are derived display strings, not actual pod phases.

troubleshoot.q: A pod is stuck Pending, and `kubectl get pvc` shows its claim status as Pending. What's the likely explanation?
o: The Service selector doesn't match the pod's labels
The pod is waiting on an unbound PersistentVolumeClaim, and it will sit in Pending indefinitely until the PVC binds
The container image doesn't exist in the registry
The node's kubelet certificate has expired
troubleshoot.x: An unbound PVC produces the event 'pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims' and keeps the pod Pending forever.

troubleshoot.q:
A pod restarts repeatedly and `kubectl describe pod` shows:
Last State:     Terminated
  Reason:       OOMKilled
  Exit Code:    137
Restart Count:  4
What is the correct interpretation?
o: The scheduler evicted the pod due to insufficient CPU
This is a generic application error unrelated to memory; check --previous logs for a stack trace
The kernel's OOM killer sent SIGKILL because the container exceeded its memory limit — fix is right-sizing the limit or the leak, not restarting harder
Exit code 137 always means a graceful SIGTERM shutdown, which is normal and needs no action
troubleshoot.x: 137 = 128+9 = SIGKILL, and Reason: OOMKilled confirms the memory-limit enforcement, not a graceful shutdown.

troubleshoot.q: What is the fundamental mistake in the reasoning 'the pod is in CrashLoopBackOff, so I'd restart it'?
o: Restarting risks permanently corrupting the underlying PersistentVolume
CrashLoopBackOff pods should always be scaled to zero replicas first
Restarting a CrashLoopBackOff pod is impossible because kubectl delete is disabled on it
CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom, not a cause — the kubelet is already restarting it; the real diagnosis is the exit code plus kubectl logs --previous
troubleshoot.x: This is the card's explicit trap: the state only says 'it keeps dying', restarting harder is exactly what's already happening.

troubleshoot.q: How does the kubelet's CrashLoopBackOff restart timing work?
o: Exponential backoff starting at 10s, doubling up to a cap of 5 minutes, with the counter resetting only after 10 minutes of clean running
A fixed 30-second delay between every restart attempt, with no cap
The delay is set by the pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds field
Immediate restart with no delay, up to a maximum of 5 attempts
troubleshoot.x: 10s, 20s, 40s... capped at 5 minutes; a crashlooping pod is mostly parked in the penalty box, not continuously crashing.

troubleshoot.q:
Given:
$ kubectl describe pod checkout-6f7d9c-tr4wp | grep -A2 Failed
  Warning  Failed  3m  kubelet  Failed to pull image "registry.corp/checkout:v2.4.1":
  rpc error: manifest for registry.corp/checkout:v2.4.1 not found
What is the diagnosis, and what should you check first?
o: The node is under DiskPressure and garbage-collected the image
The image tag v2.4.1 was never pushed (or is misspelled) — verify the tag exists in the registry rather than assuming a network or auth problem
imagePullSecrets is missing from the pod spec; add one immediately
The registry is completely unreachable from the node; check node network connectivity first
troubleshoot.x: 'manifest ... not found' points at a wrong/never-pushed tag — read the registry's actual error string before guessing.

troubleshoot.q: ImagePullBackOff can stem from three families of cause. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
o: Registry unreachable from the node (network, proxy, outage)
Wrong image name or tag (never pushed)
The container's liveness probe is misconfigured
Missing, misspelled, or expired imagePullSecrets
troubleshoot.x: ImagePullBackOff is purely about pulling the image; probes are irrelevant to it.

troubleshoot.q: A private image pull fails with 'manifest unknown', identical to what you'd see for a genuine tag typo. Why can this be misleading?
o: This error code is specific to public registries and cannot occur with private ones
This error only ever means the tag was mistyped, never an auth issue
Private registries always return a distinct 'unauthorized' error, never 'not found'
A private image with no pull secret produces the same 'not found'-style error as a typo, because registries hide private repos from unauthenticated requests
troubleshoot.x: Registries deliberately don't reveal that a private repo exists to an unauthenticated caller.

troubleshoot.q: A pod is stuck in ContainerCreating for several minutes and `kubectl describe pod` shows 'FailedCreatePodSandBox ... failed to set up pod network'. What subsystem should you suspect?
o: The CNI plugin — e.g. a crashed CNI daemonset or exhausted pod CIDR/IP space
The container registry's authentication layer
The application's own readiness probe
The PersistentVolume's storage class
troubleshoot.x: Sandbox creation failures about pod networking point straight at the CNI plugin.

troubleshoot.q: What does `MountVolume.SetUp failed ... secret "x" not found` in pod events point to?
o: An expired kubelet TLS certificate
The pod references a ConfigMap or Secret that doesn't exist in that namespace, blocking sandbox creation
A NetworkPolicy blocking egress traffic
The container exceeded its ephemeral storage limit
troubleshoot.x: This is a FailedMount event citing a missing referenced object by name.

troubleshoot.q:
You force-delete a stuck-Terminating pod on a node you've confirmed is dead using `kubectl delete pod --grace-period=0 --force`. Why do interviewers ask whether you'd do the same for a StatefulSet pod?

$ kubectl get pods -n prod
NAME        READY STATUS       RESTARTS AGE
orders-db-1 1/1   Terminating  0        3h
o: StatefulSet pods can never be deleted, only scaled down
Force-delete is disabled entirely for StatefulSets by RBAC defaults
Force-deleting lets the controller create a duplicate identity while the old pod's processes might still be running — a split-brain risk for stateful workloads like databases
Force-delete triggers an automatic full-cluster backup for StatefulSets, which is expensive
troubleshoot.x: StatefulSets deliberately refuse to replace pods on unreachable nodes for exactly this reason.

troubleshoot.q: During a node's disk-pressure incident, you later see a long list of pods in Failed state with Reason: Evicted. What produced them?
o: A NetworkPolicy denied traffic to these pods, causing them to be marked Failed
The scheduler rejected these pods for insufficient memory before they ever ran
The Deployment's progressDeadlineSeconds expired, marking old pods as Evicted
The kubelet performed node-pressure eviction, killing pods locally to reclaim resources — prioritizing pods over their requests and BestEffort pods first
troubleshoot.x: Node-pressure eviction is the kubelet's local self-defense mechanism, distinct from scheduling rejection.

troubleshoot.q: Which pods are safest from node-pressure eviction, and why?
o: Guaranteed-QoS pods (requests == limits), because eviction ranks pods first by whether usage exceeds requests, then priority, then relative usage
Pods running as DaemonSets, which are always immune regardless of QoS class
Pods with the most restart events, since the kubelet deprioritizes disruptive terminations
Pods with no resource requests set at all, since they have nothing to exceed
troubleshoot.x: BestEffort pods (zero requests) always 'exceed' their requests and die first; Guaranteed pods are most protected.

troubleshoot.q: A pod shows `Init:CrashLoopBackOff` in `kubectl get pods`. What does this specifically mean, and what command do you run next?
o: This state is cosmetic only and resolves itself once the app container starts
An init container is crashing before the main app container ever starts; run kubectl logs <pod> -c <init-container-name>
The main application container is crashing; run kubectl logs <pod> --previous
The pod failed scheduling because of an init-container-specific taint; check kubectl describe node
troubleshoot.x: Init containers run sequentially to completion before app containers start; a crashing one blocks everything.

troubleshoot.q:
Given:
$ kubectl get nodes
NAME     STATUS     ROLES   AGE   VERSION
node-a2  NotReady   <none> 212d  v1.29.4
$ kubectl describe node node-a2
Conditions:
  Type  Status  Reason  Message
  Ready Unknown NodeStatusUnknown  Kubelet stopped posting node status.
Taints: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute
What should you do first?
o: Delete the node object right away to force pod rescheduling
Restart every pod that was running on node-a2 manually
Diagnose why the kubelet stopped reporting (journalctl -u kubelet, runtime, CNI, certs, disk) and cordon to contain — don't drain a node whose kubelet may be dead
Immediately run kubectl drain node-a2 --ignore-daemonsets to evict everything gracefully
troubleshoot.x: You can't gracefully drain a node whose kubelet is dead — evictions can't be confirmed; diagnose first, then contain.

troubleshoot.q: What is the practical difference between kubectl cordon and kubectl drain?
o: cordon evicts pods immediately; drain only prevents new pods from scheduling
cordon works on nodes; drain only works on individual pods
They are aliases for the same operation in modern kubectl versions
cordon only marks the node unschedulable, leaving existing pods running; drain cordons AND evicts pods gracefully, honoring PodDisruptionBudgets
troubleshoot.x: cordon = 'stop the bleeding, I suspect this node'; drain = the full pre-maintenance eviction.

troubleshoot.q:
Given:
$ kubectl drain node-a3 --ignore-daemonsets
evicting pod prod/orders-db-1
error when evicting pods/"orders-db-1": Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.
What is happening and what are legitimate fixes?
