o: A PodDisruptionBudget is blocking the voluntary eviction; scale the app up so a disruption becomes affordable, fix an overly strict PDB, or as a break-glass option, delete the pod directly (which bypasses PDBs)
The node is already fully drained and this is a stale cache error; retry the same command
This means the node is NotReady and drain cannot function until it recovers
PodDisruptionBudgets never block drain, so this must be a kube-proxy bug
troubleshoot.x: This is a feature, not a bug — the PDB is protecting availability; check kubectl get pdb -A for ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS: 0.

troubleshoot.q: A node shows Ready=Unknown with 'Kubelet stopped posting node status', versus another node showing MemoryPressure=True. How should you interpret the difference?
o: True pressure conditions are cosmetic and don't require any action
Unknown means the node controller lost contact entirely — go look at the machine; a specific True pressure condition means go look at that resource on an otherwise-reachable node
Unknown always means the node has been manually cordoned
Both indicate exactly the same underlying problem: insufficient memory
troubleshoot.x: Unknown = node controller lost contact; a named True condition = the kubelet is actively reporting a specific problem.

troubleshoot.q: What is the documented dependency-order checklist for diagnosing a NotReady node?
o: Check kubectl top node first, since resource usage is always the root cause
Disk space → CNI → node reachable → kubelet running → container runtime → certs
Node reachable → kubelet running (systemctl/journalctl) → container runtime alive → CNI initialized → kubelet client cert validity → disk space
Only check journalctl -u kubelet; all other checks are redundant
troubleshoot.x: Diagnosis runs bottom-up through the kubelet's dependency chain.

troubleshoot.q:
Given:
$ kubectl get pod orders-db-1 -n prod
NAME        READY STATUS      RESTARTS AGE
orders-db-1 1/1   Terminating 0        6m
$ kubectl get node node-b7
NAME     STATUS   AGE
node-b7  NotReady 212d
After node-b7 died uncontrolled, how long by default before this pod is evicted, and why might a StatefulSet pod stay stuck longer than a Deployment pod would?
o: Eviction happens instantly (0s) for both Deployments and StatefulSets
The default is 30 seconds, matching terminationGracePeriodSeconds, and both controllers behave identically
StatefulSet pods are evicted faster than Deployment pods because they hold PersistentVolumes

The default tolerationSeconds is 300s (~5 min); Deployments create replacements anyway, but StatefulSets refuse to until the node is deleted or the pod force-deleted, to avoid duplicate identity / split-brain on shared volumes
troubleshoot.x: The unreachable NoExecute taint carries a default 300s tolerationSeconds; StatefulSets deliberately wait longer to avoid split-brain.

troubleshoot.q: Why does `kubectl drain` require the `--ignore-daemonsets` flag to proceed?
o: DaemonSet pods would just be recreated on the same node immediately, so draining refuses to proceed without explicitly acknowledging that
Without the flag, drain deletes the DaemonSet controller itself
DaemonSets are immune to eviction by design and the flag is purely cosmetic
The flag disables PodDisruptionBudget checks for faster draining
troubleshoot.x: Evicting a DaemonSet pod is pointless since the controller immediately recreates it on the same node.

troubleshoot.q: You need to inspect journalctl and systemd status on a node in a managed cluster (EKS/GKE/AKS) where SSH access is disabled. What's the documented approach?
o: Use kubectl exec on a random pod already running on that node
kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox, which mounts the host filesystem at /host so you can chroot in and read logs without SSH
Request emergency SSH access from the cloud provider's support team
There is no way to inspect a managed node's system logs without SSH
troubleshoot.x: This is often the ONLY way to read kubelet logs when node SSH is disabled.

troubleshoot.q: A node has DiskPressure=True. What is the kubelet's first response, before it starts evicting pods?
o: Rebooting the node's container runtime
Immediately evicting all BestEffort pods regardless of other options
Garbage collection — deleting dead containers and unused images — and only evicting pods if that fails to relieve pressure
Cordoning every other healthy node in the cluster as a precaution
troubleshoot.x: GC is tried first against both nodefs and imagefs before any pod eviction happens.

troubleshoot.q: During a large-scale outage where a big fraction of nodes in a zone go NotReady simultaneously, what does the node controller do differently compared to a single node dying?
o: It disables all PodDisruptionBudgets cluster-wide until the incident resolves
It automatically triggers a full cluster autoscale-up regardless of resource needs
It immediately force-deletes every pod on every NotReady node to restore capacity as fast as possible
It rate-limits and backs off evicting pods, assuming a network partition or control-plane problem rather than mass node death, to avoid a self-inflicted total outage
troubleshoot.x: Kubernetes deliberately hesitates during large-scale failure rather than compounding it with mass eviction.

troubleshoot.q:
Given:
$ kubectl get pods -l app=web -o wide
NAME                   READY STATUS  RESTARTS AGE IP
web-59d4c7d6b8-fk2xp   0/1   Running 0        8m  10.244.1.17
$ kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web
NAME      ADDRESSTYPE PORTS ENDPOINTS AGE
web-b8dxl IPv4        8080  <unset>   42d
$ kubectl describe pod web-59d4c7d6b8-fk2xp | grep -A1 Readiness
  Warning Unhealthy 90s (x24 over 8m) kubelet
  Readiness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.1.17:8080/healthz": dial tcp: connect: connection refused
What's the diagnosis for 'service gets no traffic'?
o: The readiness probe is failing (READY 0/1), so the pod is removed from Service endpoints even though it's Running — this is not a networking or ingress issue
The Service selector doesn't match the pod's labels at all
The node's kube-proxy has stale iptables rules
The ingress controller is down and needs a restart
troubleshoot.x: 0/1 READY plus empty endpoints is the signature of a failing readiness probe, not a selector or ingress problem.

troubleshoot.q: What's the key behavioral difference between a failing readiness probe and a failing liveness probe?
o: Liveness failure only affects DaemonSets, never Deployments
Readiness failure leaves the container running but removes it from Service endpoints (READY 0/1, RESTARTS flat); liveness failure kills and restarts the container (RESTARTS climbing)
They are functionally identical; both restart the container
Readiness failure always triggers a node cordon
troubleshoot.x: Opposite signatures and opposite blast radii — readiness quietly deregisters, liveness kills and restarts.

troubleshoot.q: Why should a liveness probe never be pointed at an external dependency (e.g., a database health check)?
o: Liveness probes are technically incapable of making outbound network calls
It would cause the Service's endpoints to be permanently deleted
A dependency outage would cause kubelet to kill and restart otherwise-healthy pods across the whole fleet simultaneously — liveness should only check 'am I deadlocked'
Dependency checks in liveness probes are automatically ignored by kubelet
troubleshoot.x: Readiness checks 'can I serve'; liveness checks only 'am I deadlocked' — mixing them causes mass unnecessary restarts.

troubleshoot.q: A Service has targetPort 80 but the app actually listens on 8080. What symptom does this produce?
o: The Service will report a validation error at apply time and refuse to create
kube-proxy silently corrects the port automatically
The Service will simply not create any endpoints at all
Endpoints exist (pod is Ready) but connections are refused — a port mismatch, distinct from a selector problem
troubleshoot.x: targetPort must match the container's actual listening port; a mismatch produces endpoints that refuse every connection.

troubleshoot.q: What is the recommended way to distinguish whether a 502 is an ingress-config problem versus a downstream pod problem?
o: Curl the Service directly from a debug pod: if that works, it's ingress-side config; if it fails, go back down to endpoints
502 errors can only be diagnosed from cloud provider load balancer logs
Check the Deployment's replica count only
Always assume 502 means the ingress controller needs a restart
troubleshoot.x: This is the hop-by-hop elimination method the apps card recommends.

troubleshoot.q: An app inside the cluster fails with 'could not resolve db-primary', but db-primary is a Service in a different namespace than the caller. What's the most likely root cause?
o: CoreDNS is definitely down and needs to be restarted
Short Service names are namespace-scoped; cross-namespace lookups need the qualified form db-primary.<ns> or the full db-primary.<ns>.svc.cluster.local
DNS caching on the client pod needs to be cleared with kubectl rollout restart
The NetworkPolicy in the target namespace is blocking all ingress by default
troubleshoot.x: Cross-namespace short-name lookups are called out as a top-3 real-world DNS 'outage' cause.

troubleshoot.q:
You update a ConfigMap consumed by a Deployment as environment variables, but only some pods behave with the new values while others still act on the old ones:
$ kubectl get pods -l app=api -o wide
NAME              READY STATUS  RESTARTS AGE
api-6b7f9-abc12   1/1   Running 0        45d
api-6b7f9-def34   1/1   Running 2        6m
Why is this happening?
o: Environment variables from ConfigMaps are cached at the API server for exactly one hour
This only happens if the ConfigMap is mounted as a volume, never as env vars
ConfigMaps consumed as env vars are only read at container start — updating the ConfigMap does not update already-running pods' environments
This indicates a corrupted etcd write; the update needs to be reapplied
troubleshoot.x: Only pods that have restarted since the ConfigMap change (like the 6m-old one) pick up new values.

troubleshoot.q: `kubectl rollout status deployment/web` shows the rollout stuck at '1 out of 3 new replicas updated' indefinitely. What happens after progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600s) elapses, and what should you do?
o: Kubernetes automatically rolls back to the previous ReplicaSet without any action needed
The Deployment is deleted automatically to prevent further resource usage
All old pods are force-terminated immediately once the deadline passes
The Deployment's Progressing condition flips to False with Reason: ProgressDeadlineExceeded — Kubernetes does NOT auto-rollback, so you must run kubectl rollout undo yourself
troubleshoot.x: The deadline only sets a condition for your CI to gate on; rollback is manual.

troubleshoot.q: Why can users often remain unaffected while a Deployment rollout is stuck with new pods in CrashLoopBackOff?
o: The old ReplicaSet's pods are still running and serving traffic during a stuck rollout, since Kubernetes doesn't tear down working replicas until new ones are Ready
Users are only affected once the Deployment itself is deleted
A stuck rollout always pauses at 0% traffic shift by default
Kubernetes automatically load-balances only to healthy pods across all namespaces
troubleshoot.x: Rollout mechanics keep old pods serving during a stuck rollout — real operational judgment is knowing this.

troubleshoot.q: You suspect NetworkPolicy is the cause of intermittent connection timeouts, even though DNS resolves and endpoints exist. What specific misconfiguration is a classic culprit?
o: NetworkPolicies can only block ingress, never egress, so this can't be a NetworkPolicy issue
A default-deny NetworkPolicy that allows app traffic but forgets to allow UDP port 53 egress, breaking DNS resolution intermittently
NetworkPolicy changes require a full cluster restart to take effect
NetworkPolicy always blocks 100% of traffic when misconfigured, never intermittently
troubleshoot.x: Forgetting DNS egress (UDP 53) in an otherwise-correct policy is a maddeningly intermittent classic.

openshift.q: Your cluster dashboard shows `oc get co` with machine-config AVAILABLE=True PROGRESSING=False DEGRADED=True, and `oc describe co machine-config` reports Reason: RequiredPoolsFailed, 'pool worker is not ready, 1 node(s) degraded'. What is this telling you?
o: A worker node is failing to apply its rendered MachineConfig, so the Machine Config Operator can't finish rolling out the pool
The API server is unreachable
etcd quorum has been lost
The OAuth identity provider is misconfigured
openshift.x: 'oc get co' is the top-level health check; Degraded=True with RequiredPoolsFailed points straight at the Machine Config Operator failing to converge a MachineConfigPool because a node in it is degraded.

openshift.q: You edit a config file directly on a node via 'oc debug node/... ' + chroot, and shortly after the change silently disappears. Why?
o: The node ran out of disk and rebooted
The Machine Config Operator detects drift from the declarative MachineConfig and reverts manual edits; you should change the MachineConfig/operator CR instead
RHCOS's SELinux policy blocked the write only temporarily
The change requires 'oc apply' to persist, not a raw file edit
openshift.x: Node config is declarative via MachineConfig objects owned by the MCO. Manual edits are drift and get reconciled away; the supported change is editing the MachineConfig itself.

openshift.q: When a self-service user runs `oc new-project team-b`, the request goes through the projectrequest API and instantiates a project template. What does this primarily stamp onto the resulting namespace that later drives SCC behavior?
o: A NetworkPolicy that blocks all egress by default
A ResourceQuota capping the project to one pod
Annotations like openshift.io/sa.scc.uid-range that drive arbitrary-UID assignment for pods in that project
An RBAC ClusterRoleBinding granting admin to all users
openshift.x: The project template stamps annotations such as openshift.io/sa.scc.uid-range, which is exactly what the SCC admission plugin reads to assign an arbitrary UID.

openshift.q: A Project object in OpenShift is best described as:
o: A separate resource unrelated to Kubernetes namespaces, used only for billing
A synonym for a MachineConfigPool
A CRD that fully replaces RBAC RoleBindings
A Kubernetes namespace with OpenShift metadata layered on, created via a template (e.g. UID range annotations, quotas)
openshift.x: A Project is literally a namespace plus OpenShift metadata stamped by the project template — same underlying object, extra annotations and request flow.

openshift.q: You push a MachineConfig adding a kernel argument to the worker MachineConfigPool. Minutes later every worker node starts cordoning, draining, and rebooting one at a time, even though you only meant to change a config value. Why?
o: The Machine Config Operator applies MachineConfig changes to a pool by cordoning, draining, and rebooting each node in turn — a rolling reboot is expected behavior, not a bug
MachineConfigPools only trigger reboots if Progressing=True is set manually first
This only happens if the MachineConfig targets the master pool
A kernel argument change always requires a full cluster reinstall
openshift.x: Applying a MachineConfig to a pool causes the MCO to roll every node in that pool through cordon/drain/reboot, one at a time — a well-known surprise for people expecting a simple file push.

openshift.q: Which single command gives the fastest top-level health check of an OpenShift cluster, showing Available/Progressing/Degraded for every platform component?
o: oc get pods -A
oc get co (clusteroperators)
oc adm top nodes
oc get events -A
openshift.x: 'oc get co' lists ClusterOperators with their Available/Progressing/Degraded conditions — the OCP equivalent of a top-level dashboard.

openshift.q: An upgrade appears stuck: `oc get co` shows the ingress operator sitting at Progressing=True far longer than expected. What's the correct next diagnostic step?
o: Delete the ingress operator pod to force a restart
Edit the IngressController Operator's Deployment directly to fix it
Run `oc describe co ingress` and check the pods in its operator/operand namespace for the actual failure reason
Roll back the ClusterVersion to force a re-sync
openshift.x: 'oc describe co <name>' plus the operator's pods in its openshift-* namespace is the documented way to find out why a stuck operator isn't converging.

openshift.q: RHCOS nodes in OpenShift are managed how?
o: Via a standard cloud-init script run once at boot
Via SSH and manual package management like any RHEL server
Via Helm charts applied to each node
Immutably, via Ignition and MachineConfigs — you generally cannot 'yum install' packages directly on a running node
openshift.x: RHCOS is treated as immutable, operator-managed configuration via Ignition + MachineConfigs, not a server you patch by hand.

openshift.q: Your security team wants only a CI pipeline (not any authenticated user) to be able to create new projects on a hardened OpenShift cluster. What's the supported fix?
o: Remove the self-provisioner ClusterRole binding from system:authenticated:oauth and customize the project request template
Delete the projectrequest API endpoint entirely
Set a ResourceQuota of 0 projects per user
Disable the OAuth server
openshift.x: The documented governance pattern is removing self-provisioner from system:authenticated:oauth so only a pipeline/admin creates projects from a vetted template.

openshift.q: An image that runs perfectly on Docker/kind CrashLoops on OpenShift with permission-denied (EACCES) errors writing to /var/lib/app, a directory the image chowned to UID 1000 at build time. What's the root cause?
o: The image's base OS is incompatible with RHCOS
restricted-v2 assigns the pod an arbitrary UID from the project's uid-range annotation, and that UID doesn't own directories chowned to UID 1000 in the image
The PVC was mounted read-only by default
OpenShift blocks all writes under /var for security
openshift.x: restricted-v2 runs pods as a random UID from the namespace's uid-range annotation; directories baked to a fixed UID (like 1000) are unwritable to that arbitrary UID.

openshift.q: What's the recommended Dockerfile fix so an image works correctly under any arbitrary UID OpenShift assigns?
o: Set USER 0 in the Dockerfile so the container always runs as root
chgrp -R 0 and chmod -R g=u on the app directories, so group 0 (which every assigned UID belongs to) can read/write them
Add the image's UID to the restricted-v2 SCC's users list
Mount an emptyDir over every directory the app writes to
openshift.x: OpenShift always adds the arbitrary UID to group 0; chgrp -R 0 + chmod -R g=u makes app directories writable regardless of which UID is assigned.

openshift.q: `oc describe rs` shows: 'unable to validate against any security context constraint... runAsUser: Invalid value: 0'. What does this admission error mean?
o: The cluster is out of available UIDs in the project's range
The service account referenced by the pod doesn't exist
The node's kubelet certificate expired
The pod (or its image) requests UID 0 (root), which restricted-v2 forbids — the image needs an arbitrary-UID-compatible fix, not a root grant
openshift.x: restricted-v2 rejects runAsUser=0. The senior fix is correcting the image's ownership assumptions, not granting a permissive SCC.

openshift.q: Which SCC is intended only for infrastructure daemonsets like CNI plugins, storage drivers, and node exporters that genuinely need to manage the host?
o: privileged
anyuid
nonroot-v2
restricted-v2
openshift.x: privileged is the 'nuclear' SCC — privileged mode, host namespaces/paths, all capabilities, any UID — reserved for genuine infrastructure daemonsets.

openshift.q: A security audit flags that the 'default' service account in a project was granted the anyuid SCC. Why is this a serious finding?
o: anyuid disables network policies for the namespace
anyuid has priority 10, which outranks restricted-v2, so every pod using that service account in the project silently becomes eligible for root-capable admission
anyuid grants cluster-admin RBAC automatically
anyuid is only a naming label with no functional effect
openshift.x: anyuid's priority 10 outranks restricted-v2, so granting it broadly (e.g. to a project's default SA) silently captures every pod in that project.

openshift.q: When multiple SCCs could admit the same pod, in what order does OpenShift's admission plugin pick one?
o: Alphabetically by name only
Whichever SCC was created most recently
Highest priority first, then most restrictive, then alphabetically by name
Random selection among eligible SCCs for load balancing
openshift.x: SCC selection sorts eligible candidates by priority (highest wins), then most restrictive, then name — the exact tie-breaking order documented for SCC admission.

openshift.q: You need to run a third-party vendor image that hardcodes `USER 1001` with matching file ownership baked in, and you cannot rebuild it. What's the narrowest SCC to grant its service account?
o: anyuid
privileged
restricted-v2 — no grant is needed
nonroot-v2, since it allows any explicit non-zero UID without the namespace uid-range restriction
openshift.x: nonroot-v2 is the documented middle ground for vendor images with a hardcoded non-zero UID — narrower than anyuid, and restricted-v2 would still force a mismatched arbitrary UID.

openshift.q: A pod is admitted by restricted-v2 but events also show a Pod Security warning: 'would violate PodSecurity restricted:latest'. What does this indicate?
o: Both SCCs and Kubernetes Pod Security Admission run on OpenShift; PSA labels are synced from available SCCs and can emit warnings even when the SCC is what actually enforces/admits the pod
The pod was actually rejected and never scheduled
PSA has fully replaced SCCs on this cluster
The warning means the SCC configuration is corrupted and must be recreated
openshift.x: SCCs and PSA coexist on OpenShift; PSA warn/audit labels are synced from the SCCs available to a namespace's service accounts, so a warning can appear even though the SCC is the actual enforcement mechanism.

openshift.q: A pod using a PVC under restricted-v2 still fails to write to the mounted volume even after fixing directory group ownership inside the image. What's the likely missing piece?
o: The PVC's storage class doesn't support ReadWriteMany
pod.spec.securityContext.fsGroup isn't set (or falls outside the namespace's openshift.io/sa.scc.supplemental-groups range), so the volume was never chowned to a group the arbitrary UID belongs to
The SCC needs to be changed to privileged
fsGroup only applies to hostPath volumes, not PVCs
openshift.x: For PVCs, fsGroup drives the kubelet to chown/chmod the mounted volume; under restricted-v2 it must also fall within the namespace's supplemental-groups range.

openshift.q: You create a Route for www.example.com but browsers show a certificate warning for the cluster's default *.apps wildcard domain instead of your company's cert. What's the most likely cause?
o: The Route's Service has no ready endpoints
You used passthrough termination, which always ignores custom domains
You created the Route without specifying edge termination cert/key (or DNS points at the wrong router shard), so the router served its default wildcard cert
OpenShift caches certificates for 24 hours before applying them
openshift.x: Seeing the *.apps wildcard cert for a custom domain maps to an edge route created without cert/key (or DNS pointing at the wrong shard) — exactly the documented cert-failure-to-mode mapping.

openshift.q: A Route returns 'Application is not available' — a page served by the router itself — even though the app's Deployment looks fine. Where should you look first?
o: The BuildConfig logs for the last build
The ClusterVersion Operator's upgrade status
The project's ResourceQuota for CPU
The Service's selector, targetPort vs containerPort, and pod readiness — the router has the route admitted but no ready endpoints to send traffic to
openshift.x: 'Application is not available' is served BY the router when it has the route but no ready endpoints; check Service selector, ports, and readiness first, not the app.

openshift.q: Your app needs mutual TLS (mTLS) directly between the client and the pod, with the pod itself terminating TLS. Which Route TLS mode fits?
o: Passthrough
Edge
Re-encrypt
None — Routes can't carry TLS all the way to the pod
openshift.x: Passthrough never decrypts at the router; TLS (including mTLS) flows through via SNI, which is required when the app itself must terminate TLS.

openshift.q: Under re-encrypt termination, how does the router avoid needing an explicit destinationCACertificate on the Route while still trusting the backend's serving cert?
o: The router trusts any self-signed cert on the internal SDN by default
By annotating the Service with service.beta.openshift.io/serving-cert-secret-name, so the service-ca operator mints/rotates a serving cert the router trusts by default
destinationCACertificate is never required for re-encrypt routes
By setting insecureEdgeTerminationPolicy: Allow
openshift.x: The service-ca operator's serving-cert-secret-name annotation mints a cert signed by the cluster's service CA, which the router trusts by default — the standard 'encrypted end-to-end, zero cert toil' combo.

openshift.q: A re-encrypt Route returns 503 even though the pods are healthy and `curl localhost` inside the pod works fine. What's the most likely cause?
o: The pod's liveness probe is misconfigured
The BuildConfig failed on its last push
The router (acting as a TLS client to the pod) can't validate the backend's serving cert — expired cert, SAN mismatch after a service rename, or wrong destinationCACertificate
The project ran out of image pull secrets
openshift.x: On re-encrypt, the router is the TLS client to the pod; a cert validation failure there produces exactly this symptom — 503 at the route while the app itself is fine.

openshift.q: Team A creates a Route for shared.example.com in a scratch namespace. Weeks later Team B tries to create a production Route with the same hostname in their own namespace and it's rejected. Why?
o: Hostnames must be unique per cluster only for edge termination
DNS records, not OpenShift, own hostname uniqueness
Only cluster-admins can create Routes with custom hostnames

Route admission enforces hostname uniqueness — the oldest route claims the host, and a later route with the same host is rejected as HostAlreadyClaimed unless routeAdmission allows InterNamespaceAllowed
openshift.x: Route admission enforces hostname uniqueness cluster-wide; the oldest route wins and later duplicates are rejected unless cross-namespace sharing is explicitly allowed.

openshift.q: How does OpenShift implement the standard Kubernetes Ingress API under the hood?
o: The router/Ingress Operator translates admitted Ingress objects into Route objects behind the scenes, so both Ingress and Route resources work
Ingress objects are rejected outright; only Route objects are supported
OpenShift runs a separate nginx-ingress controller alongside the HAProxy router for Ingress objects
Ingress objects are converted into NetworkPolicies, not Routes
openshift.x: Ingress objects work on OpenShift because the router translates admitted Ingress into Route objects behind the scenes, visible via ownerReferences.

openshift.q: Long-polling/websocket-like requests through a Route start failing with 504s after about 30 seconds, even though the backend is still working. What's the fix?
o: Switch the Route from edge to passthrough termination
Set the haproxy.router.openshift.io/timeout annotation on the Route to extend HAProxy's default server timeout
Increase the pod's memory limit
Add more replicas to the Deployment
openshift.x: HAProxy's default server timeout (30s) is the classic cause of premature 504s on long polls; fix per-route with the haproxy.router.openshift.io/timeout annotation.

openshift.q: Per-tenant subdomain routes (spec.wildcardPolicy: Subdomain) are:
o: Enabled by default on every IngressController
Only available with passthrough termination
Disabled by default; the IngressController must explicitly set routeAdmission.wildcardPolicy to WildcardsAllowed
A feature of DeploymentConfigs, not Routes
openshift.x: Wildcard routes are disabled by default and require the IngressController's routeAdmission.wildcardPolicy to be set to WildcardsAllowed.

openshift.q: A developer says: 'we pushed v2 to the registry but prod is still running v1.' What's the correct troubleshooting order to find the broken link?
o: Immediately restart the Deployment's pods
Assume the BuildConfig is broken and re-run 'oc new-app'
Check the SCC assigned to the deployment's service account

Check whether the registry digest was actually re-imported into the ImageStreamTag, whether a trigger is wired from that tag to the Deployment, and whether the rollout actually fired — the chain is registry digest -> istag import -> trigger -> rollout
openshift.x: Each hop is separately wired; the documented debug approach is walking the chain registry digest -> istag import -> trigger -> rollout to find exactly which joint broke.

openshift.q: How does an S2I (source-to-image) build produce an image without a Dockerfile?
o: A builder image's 'assemble' script injects and compiles/installs the source code into a copy of the builder image, then the 'run' script becomes the entrypoint
OpenShift auto-generates a Dockerfile from the source and builds it with buildah
It uses a hidden default Dockerfile shipped with every builder image
It copies the source directly into a fixed base image with no build step at all
openshift.x: S2I injects source into a builder image and runs its assemble script to produce the final image, with the run script as entrypoint — no Dockerfile involved.

openshift.q: You're migrating an old app from a DeploymentConfig to a Deployment. Which behavior difference is most likely to bite you?
o: Deployments don't support rolling updates at all

DeploymentConfigs use ReplicationControllers and can have image triggers with automatic:false (silently not deploying on tag moves); Deployments need the image.openshift.io/triggers annotation to get equivalent ImageStreamTag integration
DeploymentConfigs can't be scaled with 'oc scale'
Only Deployments support S2I builds
openshift.x: DCs use ReplicationControllers and can silently skip deploys with automatic:false; Deployments need the image.openshift.io/triggers annotation to replicate ImageStreamTag-driven rollouts.

openshift.q: A Deployment in project app-prod shows ImagePullBackOff pulling an internal ImageStream image that lives in project shared-images. What's the canonical fix?
o: Copy the image into the internal registry's root namespace
Grant the service account the anyuid SCC
Grant the app-prod service account the system:image-puller role in the shared-images project
Set the ImageStream's referencePolicy to source
openshift.x: Cross-project pulls of internal images need explicit RBAC: granting system:image-puller in the source project to the consuming SA is the documented fix for cross-namespace ImagePullBackOff.

openshift.q: What does `oc tag quay.io/org/app:v2 web:prod --scheduled` do?
o: Immediately and permanently copies the image into the internal registry, one time only
Schedules a BuildConfig to run nightly
Creates a CronJob that redeploys the app every 15 minutes
Makes the cluster periodically (roughly every ~15 minutes) poll the external registry and re-import the tag into the ImageStream when its digest changes
openshift.x: --scheduled makes the cluster poll the external registry on an interval (about 15 minutes) and re-import when the digest changes, as opposed to a one-time 'oc import-image'.

openshift.q: Your cluster keeps hitting Docker Hub rate limits because every pod pulls an external image directly. What ImageStream setting addresses this?
o: Set referencePolicy to 'local' so pulls are rewritten through the internal registry, which caches the image and buffers against external rate-limiting/outages
Set referencePolicy to 'source' so pods always pull from the origin registry
Disable the ImageStream and use raw image strings instead
Increase the project's ResourceQuota for pods
openshift.x: referencePolicy: local routes pulls through the internal registry's cache — the documented standard answer to Docker Hub rate-limit incidents.

openshift.q: What's OpenShift's native answer to a multi-stage Docker build when the S2I builder alone would ship a fat toolchain?
o: A single S2I build using a 'slim' variant of every builder image
A chained build: a first S2I build compiles with the full toolchain, then a second Docker-strategy build copies just the artifact into a slim runtime image via source images
Passing --squash to 'oc start-build'
Using a DeploymentConfig lifecycle hook to strip the toolchain post-deploy
openshift.x: Chained builds — an S2I compile step feeding a Docker-strategy image via source images — are the documented native equivalent of multi-stage Docker builds.

openshift.q: Several otherwise-green builds start failing right at the final push step, and you suspect the internal registry's storage is full from accumulated layers. What's the day-2 fix?
o: Increase every BuildConfig's completionDeadlineSeconds
Switch all builds from S2I to Docker strategy
Run 'oc adm prune images' (and 'oc adm prune builds', or an ImagePruner CR for scheduled pruning) to reclaim registry storage
Delete and recreate all ImageStreams
openshift.x: Pruning is the documented day-2 duty for this exact symptom: registry-full presents as failed pushes at the end of otherwise-green builds; 'oc adm prune images'/builds or a scheduled ImagePruner CR fixes it.

sre.q: Your service has a 99.9% availability SLO over a rolling 30-day window. How many minutes of full downtime does the error budget allow per window?
o: 4.32 minutes
43.2 minutes
21.6 minutes
14.4 minutes
sre.x: 30 days = 43,200 minutes; the budget is (1 - 0.999) x 43,200 = 43.2 minutes. Each extra nine divides the budget by ten: 99.99% would allow only 4.32 minutes.

sre.q: Which of these is a well-formed SLI in the canonical SRE shape?
o: Average CPU utilization across the fleet stays below 80%
The p99 latency graph looks flat during business hours
Requests returning non-5xx in under 300 ms, divided by total requests, measured at the load balancer
Number of deploys per week that required a rollback
sre.x: The canonical SLI is good events / total events with a precise definition of both, measured at a stated point. CPU is a cause metric users never see, and the others lack the good/total ratio structure.

sre.q: Your team's SLO is 99.9%, but for six straight months you've delivered 99.99%. According to the SRE book, what risk are you running?
o: Users and dependent teams build on the implicit 99.99%, so a normal 99.9% month now breaks them
None — over-delivering on an SLO is always pure upside
The monitoring system will recalibrate the SLO upward automatically
The error budget will roll over and encourage reckless deploys next quarter
sre.x: This is the Chubby lesson: dependents assume the delivered level, not the promised one. Google deliberately took Chubby down to burn budget and flush out hidden dependencies. Budgets don't roll over and SLOs don't auto-adjust.

sre.q: An error budget policy typically specifies what consequence when the 30-day budget is fully exhausted?
o: The SLO is lowered until the budget recovers
On-call staffing is doubled for the next month
All alerts are temporarily rerouted to tickets
Feature releases freeze and engineering effort shifts to reliability work
sre.x: The policy is a pre-agreed contract: budget remaining means dev ships at will; budget exhausted means releases pause and reliability work takes priority until the rolling window recovers. It converts the dev-vs-ops argument into arithmetic.

sre.q: Your backend metrics show 100% success, but users report the site is down. Which SLI measurement-point mistake most plausibly explains this?
o: The SLO window is calendar-month instead of rolling
You measure only at the application servers, missing failures at the load balancer, DNS, or client side
You included health-check traffic in the total-events denominator
You set the latency threshold at p95 instead of p99
sre.x: Server-side metrics can't see requests that never arrive (LB overload, DNS, TLS) or client-side failures like a broken JS bundle. The SRE book recommends measuring close to the user, supplementing server metrics with client-side or black-box probes.

sre.q: How many minutes of monthly downtime does a 99.95% SLO allow over 30 days?
o: 21.6 minutes
43.2 minutes
10.8 minutes
4.32 minutes
sre.x: 0.05% of 43,200 minutes = 21.6 minutes — exactly half the 99.9% budget. Interviewers expect the ladder: 99.9% = 43.2 min, 99.95% = 21.6 min, 99.99% = 4.32 min.

sre.q: You're setting the first SLO for a new API. Per the SRE book, the target should primarily be based on what?
o: Whatever availability the service achieved over its last quarter
The tightest number engineering believes is technically achievable
What users actually need from the service
The highest SLA any competitor publishes
sre.x: Start from user needs, not current performance — basing the target on today's dashboard enshrines accidents as promises. Current performance informs feasibility, but the objective is derived from what users require.

sre.q: Error budget math: on a 99.9% SLO over 30 days (720 hours), a burn rate of 6 sustained for its full 6-hour alert window consumes how much budget?
sre.x: Budget consumed = burn rate x window / period = 6 x 6h / 720h = 5%. The same math gives 14.4 x 1/720 = 2% for the fast tier and 1 x 72/720 = 10% for the 3-day ticket tier.

sre.q: In multiwindow multi-burn-rate alerting, why pair the 1-hour long window with a 5-minute short window that must ALSO exceed the threshold?
o: The short window raises recall by catching slower burns
It lets the alert fire before any budget is consumed
Prometheus cannot evaluate 1-hour range vectors reliably
It improves reset time — the alert clears quickly after recovery instead of firing while stale errors age out of the long window
sre.x: After a 15-minute outage ends, the bad data sits in the 1-hour window for ~45 more minutes. Requiring the short window to also exceed the threshold confirms you're still actively burning budget, so the alert resets within minutes. The guideline is short = 1/12 of long.

sre.q: Your on-call gets paged at 3am: 'node CPU > 90% for 10 minutes.' Error rate and latency SLIs are normal. What does SRE monitoring doctrine say about this page?
o: It's a cause-based alert with no user-visible symptom — it should be a ticket or dashboard, not a page
It's valid — saturation is a golden signal, so any CPU breach must page
The threshold should simply be raised to 95%
It should page only during business hours
sre.x: Pages should reflect symptoms — user-visible impact — while causes like CPU feed diagnosis. Saturation is worth monitoring, but a cause alert with healthy SLIs is exactly the non-actionable 3am page that breeds alert fatigue.

sre.q: What does a burn rate of exactly 1 mean?
o: The service is failing 1% of requests
The error budget was exhausted in the last hour
You're consuming budget at precisely the rate that exhausts it exactly at the end of the SLO window
No errors are occurring at all
sre.x: Burn rate is relative to the SLO period: 1x on a 30-day window means the budget lasts exactly 30 days. On a 99.9% SLO that's a steady 0.1% error rate; 2x exhausts in 15 days; a total outage is ~1000x, gone in about 43 minutes.

sre.q: A dependency is silently failing 0.12% of your requests — just above your 99.9% SLO's 0.1% budget rate. Per the SRE Workbook tiers, how should this surface?
o: A page from the 14.4x/1-hour tier
A ticket from the 1x burn-rate / 3-day window tier
It cannot be detected by burn-rate alerting at all
An immediate SEV1 incident declaration
sre.x: A ~1.2x burn is far below the paging tiers (14.4x and 6x) but the slow-burn tier — burn rate 1 over a 3-day window, 10% of budget — catches exactly this leak and files a ticket. It's urgent for the month's budget, not for 3am.

sre.q: The SRE Workbook's rule of thumb for sizing the short window relative to the long window is:
o: Short window = 1/12 of the long window
Short window = half of the long window
Short window = fixed 1 minute regardless of long window
Short window = the long window minus the sync period
sre.x: The Workbook recommends making the short window 1/12 the duration of the long one — hence the canonical pairs 1h/5m, 6h/30m, and 3d/6h.

sre.q: Which set is the SRE book's four golden signals?
o: Rate, Errors, Duration, Saturation
Utilization, Saturation, Errors, Availability
Latency, Throughput, Capacity, Cost
Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation
sre.x: Latency (split by success vs failure — fast 500s skew averages), traffic, errors, and saturation. RED (Rate/Errors/Duration) is the request-centric variant for services; USE (Utilization/Saturation/Errors) is the resource-centric one.

sre.q: A total outage begins on your 99.9%/30-day service — 100% of requests failing. Roughly how long until the entire monthly error budget is gone?
o: 30 hours
7.2 hours
About 43 minutes
3 days
sre.x: 100% errors on a 0.1% budget is a 1000x burn rate: 43,200 minutes / 1000 = 43.2 minutes to total exhaustion. This is why fast-burn tiers page within minutes.

sre.q: You're on-call and a SEV1 begins: checkout errors spiked 10 minutes after a deploy. Per Google's incident doctrine, your FIRST priority is:
o: Attach a profiler and find the root cause in the new code
Mitigate — roll back the deploy to stop user impact; root cause waits for the postmortem
Write the postmortem timeline while events are fresh
Email stakeholders a detailed technical analysis
sre.x: The priority order is stop the bleeding, restore service, then preserve evidence. Generic mitigations — rollback, feature-flag off, failover, load shedding — work before you understand the bug. Understanding is the postmortem's job.

sre.q: During a managed incident, what does the Incident Commander actually do?
o: Holds the big picture: assigns roles, tracks state, sets priorities — and deliberately does NOT debug
Personally drives the debugging session since they're most senior
Writes and sends all external customer communications
Approves each individual command run in production
sre.x: The IC's job is coordination, borrowed from the emergency-services Incident Command System. Hands-on work belongs to the Ops Lead's team; communications belong to the Comms Lead. An IC who starts debugging abandons the big picture.

sre.q: Per the SRE book, which group should be the ONLY one modifying the production system during an incident?
o: Anyone with production access, to maximize parallelism
The Incident Commander personally
The operations team working under the Ops Lead
The service's original developers
sre.x: The SRE book states the operations team should be the only group modifying the system during an incident. Freelance fixes from the sidelines cause conflicting changes — how one outage becomes two.

sre.q: You've been debugging a production issue alone for over an hour with no resolution, and it may be customer-visible. What does Google's guidance say?
o: Keep going — declaring an incident for something you might solve soon looks bad
Escalate only if a manager approves
Wait until a second customer complaint arrives
Declare an incident now — 'unsolved after an hour' and 'customer-visible' are both explicit declaration criteria
sre.x: Google's triggers: a second team is needed, the outage is customer-visible, or the issue is unsolved after an hour of focused analysis. Declaring early is cheap; grinding solo at 3am on a real outage is not.

sre.q: It's hour six of an incident and you're handing off command before rest. What does a correct handoff look like?
o: Post 'logging off, someone take over' in the channel and disconnect
Explicitly state 'You're now the incident commander' and wait for firm acknowledgment before leaving
Update the state doc's owner field and assume it's noticed
CC the incoming IC on the last stakeholder email
sre.x: The SRE book's example is nearly verbatim: the outgoing IC says 'You're now the incident commander, okay?' and waits for explicit confirmation. Ambiguous handoffs — where everyone assumes someone else has command — are how long incidents fail.

sre.q: What is the Communications Lead's core function during an incident?
o: Issue periodic updates to stakeholders on a fixed cadence so responders aren't interrupted for status
Negotiate SLA credits with affected customers in real time
Transcribe every command run into the postmortem
Approve the Ops Lead's mitigation choices
sre.x: The Comms Lead is the public face, posting updates at a regular cadence (even 'no change, next update at :30'). This stops executives and support from pinging the people doing the work — protecting responder focus is the whole point.

sre.q: Errors began 20 minutes ago, right after a config deploy; the change diff is large and unclear. Which mitigation is usually fastest and safest?
o: Read the entire diff until you find the bug, then hotfix forward
Add more replicas to absorb the errors
Roll back the deploy immediately and analyze the diff afterward
Restart all pods to clear possible bad state
sre.x: Strong correlation with a recent change makes rollback the generic, fast, low-risk mitigation — no understanding of the bug required. Fix-forward under pressure and speculative restarts both extend user impact while you guess.

sre.q: What does 'blameless' actually mean in a blameless postmortem?
o: No individual actions are ever mentioned in the document
Assume everyone acted with good intent on the information they had, and analyze why the system made the failure possible
No one can face consequences for anything, including sabotage
The postmortem must avoid naming a root cause
sre.x: Blameless means the analysis targets the system, not the person: names and actions appear in the timeline, but the question is 'why did the pipeline allow this?' not 'why did this engineer err?'. Genuine recklessness is a management matter handled outside the document.

sre.q: After a harsh, name-and-shame incident review, what does SRE doctrine predict will happen in your organization's future incidents?
o: Engineers become more careful, so incidents get shorter
Nothing changes — review tone doesn't affect operations
More postmortems get written, improving learning
People hide problems, delay escalation, and under-report near-misses — the incident data supply collapses
sre.x: The SRE book: where finger-pointing prevails, 'people will not bring issues to light for fear of punishment.' The goal shifts from system improvement to self-protection — you pay full outage cost and receive none of the learning. This is the aviation/healthcare lesson blamelessness imports.

sre.q: Which event should trigger a postmortem even if user impact was tiny?
o: Data loss of any kind, or an incident discovered by a human rather than by monitoring
Any deploy that took longer than planned
Every on-call shift, as routine practice
A dashboard being slow to load for one engineer
sre.x: Standard triggers include ANY data loss, user-visible downtime beyond a threshold, on-call intervention, long resolution times, and monitoring failure — a human finding the incident before an alert did is itself a defect worth analyzing.

sre.q: A postmortem's action items are most likely to actually prevent recurrence if each one has:
o: A commitment from the team to 'be more careful next time'
A long list of every hypothetical failure mode
A named individual owner, a priority, and a tracked ticket — biased toward prevention and detection fixes
Sign-off from the engineer who caused the incident
sre.x: A team name as owner is nobody; 'be more careful' patches the human instead of the system and is worthless. Senior-engineer review of drafts exists partly to verify AIs are concrete, owned, and would genuinely prevent or detect recurrence.

sre.q: Your VP wants 'MTTR reduced 20% this quarter' as the team's headline reliability KPI. What's the strongest caveat you should raise?
o: MTTR can only be improved by hiring more on-callers
MTTR is defined identically everywhere, so the target is unambiguous
MTTR should be replaced with a count of postmortems written
With few, heterogeneous incidents the mean is statistically fragile — one long incident swamps it — and a targeted metric invites gaming like early closure or severity downgrades
sre.x: One 6-hour incident among nine 5-minute rollbacks doubles MTTR while signaling nothing. Distributions and per-class analysis beat single means, 'R' itself is ambiguous (repair/recover/resolve), and metrics-as-targets get gamed. Postmortem counts are worse — they punish honest declarers.

sre.q: What is Google's 'Wheel of Misfortune' exercise?
o: Role-playing past postmortems as live disaster scenarios so engineers practice incident response
Randomly assigning blame for an incident to a team member
A lottery deciding who takes the next on-call shift
Chaos-engineering tooling that kills random production pods
sre.x: Wheel of Misfortune replays real past incidents as theater — an engineer responds live while a peer plays the system — converting the postmortem archive into practiced muscle memory. It sits alongside DiRT exercises and 'Postmortem of the Month' in reinforcing the culture.

sre.q: During review, a senior engineer asks your postmortem draft: 'where did we get lucky?' Why is that section valuable?
o: It fills mandatory template space required for sign-off
It credits individual heroics so responders feel appreciated
It provides legal cover by documenting due diligence
It names latent failures that didn't fire this time — the stale-but-usable backup, the engineer who happened to be awake — so they're fixed before luck runs out
sre.x: 'Where we got lucky' surfaces near-misses inside the incident: conditions that would have made it far worse. Documenting them turns luck into action items, which is precisely the learning blameless culture is designed to extract.

sre.q: In Kubernetes HPA, 'CPU utilization: 80%' means the pod is using 80% of what?
o: The node's allocatable CPU
The pod's CPU limit
The pod's CPU resource request
The cluster's total CPU capacity
sre.x: HPA utilization = actual usage / resource REQUEST — limits play no part. A pod requesting 500m and using 400m is at 80% even with a 2-core limit. Corollary: pods without CPU requests break CPU-based HPA entirely.

sre.q: Your Deployment runs 4 replicas averaging 90% CPU-of-requests; the HPA target is 60%. How many replicas does the HPA compute?
sre.x: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetric / targetMetric) = ceil(4 x 90/60) = ceil(6.0) = 6. The controller evaluates roughly every 15s with a 10% tolerance band around ratio 1.0.

sre.q: A teammate proposes running HPA and VPA together, both driven by CPU, 'so pods are always right-sized AND right-counted.' Why is this a known anti-pattern?
o: VPA rewrites CPU requests, which instantly changes the utilization percentage HPA computes — two controllers actuating on one signal oscillate
VPA and HPA cannot be installed in the same cluster
HPA always takes precedence, so VPA becomes a silent no-op
It works fine and is the recommended default
sre.x: Because HPA utilization = usage/request, a VPA request change moves every pod's percentage with zero change in real load: VPA raises requests, utilization falls, HPA scales in, per-pod load rises, VPA raises requests again. Safe splits: HPA on CPU + VPA on memory, or HPA on a custom metric (RPS/queue depth).

sre.q: Traffic to your API spikes every few minutes with quiet gaps between. Which HPA mechanism prevents replicas being deleted during a brief lull right before the next spike?
o: The 10% tolerance band on the metric ratio
The 5-minute CPU initialization period
The Metrics Server's 15-second scrape interval
The scale-down stabilization window (default 300s), which keeps the highest recommendation from the last 5 minutes
sre.x: Scale-down uses a 300-second stabilization window by default: the HPA acts on the maximum recommendation seen in that span, so short dips don't remove capacity you're about to need. Scale-up has no default stabilization; both are tunable via the v2 behavior field.

sre.q: Your HPA scales pods up during a spike but they sit Pending for 4 minutes before serving. The cluster runs Cluster Autoscaler on fixed node groups. What's the widely-cited advantage of Karpenter here?
o: Karpenter removes the need for pod resource requests
It provisions right-sized instances directly from the pending pods' aggregate resource shapes, skipping node groups for faster, better bin-packed capacity
Karpenter scales the pods themselves, replacing the HPA
It caches pre-pulled images so pods start faster
sre.x: Cluster Autoscaler grows pre-defined node groups (e.g., ASGs); Karpenter watches pending pods and launches instance types matched to their actual aggregate needs, typically cutting provisioning latency and cost. Either way HPA -> Pending -> node scale-up is the slow chain, which is why teams add headroom or balloon pods.

sre.q: Your queue workers are I/O-bound: during a backlog, Kafka lag explodes while worker CPU stays low, so the CPU-based HPA never scales. What's the standard fix?
o: Lower the CPU target to 5% so any activity triggers scaling
Switch the HPA to memory utilization instead
Use KEDA (or an external/custom metric HPA) to scale on queue depth or consumer lag — event-driven scaling that can even go to zero
Remove CPU requests so utilization reads as infinite
sre.x: Queue depth is the true demand signal for workers; CPU lies when consumers block on I/O. KEDA provides 60+ scalers (SQS, Kafka lag, Prometheus queries, cron) and supports scale-to-zero, which vanilla HPA cannot (minReplicas >= 1). Memory is a trap since many runtimes never release it.
